pKa.desc: The negative common logarithm of the acid dissociation constant Ka. The smaller it is, the stronger the acid. Typical values: carboxylic acids about 4–5, phenol about 10, water 15.7, alcohols about 16.

about.h: What pKa means and how to read it
about.p: pKa is the negative common logarithm of the acid dissociation constant Ka (pKa = −log Ka), and it expresses how strongly an acid HA tends to release H⁺ in water and become A⁻. The larger Ka, the stronger the acid and the smaller the pKa. A difference of 1 in pKa means a tenfold difference in Ka, so acetic acid at pKa 4.8 is about 10¹¹ times stronger than ethanol at pKa 16. Values change with temperature and solvent, so comparisons normally use values in water at 25 °C. For acids too weak or too strong to measure in water, values in other solvents such as DMSO or extrapolated values are used.

Typical values used in organic chemistry are about 4–5 for carboxylic acids (acetic acid 4.76, benzoic acid 4.2), about 10 for phenol, about 16 for alcohols, 15.7 for water, about 9–11 for ammonium ions (9.25 for NH4⁺) and about 25 for terminal alkynes. Among strong acids, hydrogen chloride is about −7 and the first dissociation of sulfuric acid about −3, and protonated carbonyl compounds also have negative values. Alkane C−H bonds, by contrast, are about 50 and show almost no acidity. With these values you can quickly judge whether the base used in a reaction can deprotonate the substrate.

The equilibrium constant of the acid–base reaction HA + B⁻ ⇌ A⁻ + HB is K = 10^(pKa(HB) − pKa(HA)), and the equilibrium lies toward forming the weaker acid, the one with the larger pKa. For example, for acetic acid (4.76) and ammonia (NH4⁺ 9.25), K is about 3×10⁴ and the equilibrium lies far to the right, while for phenol (10.0) and bicarbonate ion (H2CO3 6.4), K is small, about 2.5×10⁻⁴, and they hardly react. This reasoning applies directly to separating acidic, neutral and basic substances by extraction and to choosing bases for synthesis.

The proportions of the neutral and ionized forms of a weak acid or weak base are set by the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). When the pH equals the pKa, the two are half and half; for a weak acid, at a pH one unit above the pKa the ionized form is about 91%, and two units above, about 99%. The neutral form is thought to cross lipid membranes more readily and the ionized form to dissolve in water more readily, so the absorption, distribution and solubility of drugs, and even how strongly they are retained in liquid chromatography, are considered in terms of the relationship between pKa and the surrounding pH.

faq.q: Is a smaller pKa a stronger acid?
faq.a: Yes. Because pKa = −log Ka, the larger Ka (the more readily the acid dissociates), the smaller the pKa. A pKa one unit smaller means the acid is ten times stronger in terms of Ka.

faq.q: Can base strength also be expressed with pKa?
faq.a: Base strength is generally expressed by the pKa of the conjugate acid. The larger the conjugate acid's pKa, the stronger the base; for example, ammonia (pKa of NH4⁺ 9.25) is a stronger base than aniline (pKa of the anilinium ion about 4.6).

faq.q: What is the difference between pKa and pH?
faq.a: pKa is a constant characteristic of a particular acid, while pH expresses the hydrogen-ion activity of a solution. When the pH of a solution equals the pKa of the acid, the acid is exactly half in its neutral form and half as the ionized conjugate base.

混成軌道.desc: Equivalent orbitals formed by mixing an atom's s and p orbitals. sp³ gives a tetrahedral shape (about 109.5°), sp² trigonal planar (120°) and sp linear (180°).

共鳴.desc: The idea of representing a real molecule as a superposition of several structures (resonance structures) that differ only in the arrangement of electrons. Molecules and ions with delocalized charge or π electrons are stabilized.

誘起効果.desc: The polarization of electrons through σ bonds caused by differences in electronegativity. Electron-withdrawing groups such as chlorine stabilize the conjugate base of a carboxylic acid and strengthen its acidity. It falls off sharply with distance.

ヘンダーソン・ハッセルバルヒの式.desc: The equation pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), used to find the pH of a buffer and the proportions of the neutral and ionized forms of a weak acid. At pH = pKa the two are equal.

キラリティ.desc: The property of not being superimposable on one's mirror image. A chiral molecule exists as a pair of enantiomers. It is usually caused by an asymmetric carbon, but axial chirality and other types also exist.

about.p: The property of not being superimposable on one's mirror image is called chirality, and such molecules are called chiral molecules. It is likened to the relationship between right and left hands, and the word comes from the Greek for "hand". A molecule that is superimposable on its mirror image is achiral. A chiral molecule exists as a pair of enantiomers that are mirror images of each other. Whether a molecule is chiral depends on whether it has a mirror plane or a center of symmetry (more generally, an improper rotation axis); a molecule with none of these is chiral.

The most common source of chirality is an sp³ carbon bonded to four different groups (an asymmetric carbon, or chiral center). A molecule with exactly one asymmetric carbon is always chiral, but with two or more, meso compounds that are achiral because of an internal mirror plane can appear. Conversely, some molecules are chiral without any asymmetric carbon: examples are biaryls with hindered rotation about a single bond (axial chirality), substituted allenes and helical helicenes. It is important to judge chirality by the symmetry of the whole molecule.

Enzymes and receptors in the body are made of chiral proteins, so enantiomers can act differently in the body. There are known examples in which one enantiomer has the therapeutic effect while the other is inactive or has a different action. In drug development, therefore, the enantiomers are separated and each is evaluated, and where necessary the drug is manufactured as a single enantiomer. Enantiomeric excess (ee) is used as the measure of purity and is determined by methods such as HPLC on a chiral stationary phase.

faq.q: Does a chiral molecule always have an asymmetric carbon?
faq.a: No. Some molecules, such as biaryls with axial chirality and allenes, are chiral without an asymmetric carbon. Conversely, some molecules, such as meso compounds, are achiral even though they have asymmetric carbons.

faq.q: How do you decide whether a molecule is chiral?
faq.a: Check whether the molecule has a mirror plane or a center of symmetry. If it has neither, it very likely cannot be superimposed on its mirror image and is chiral; strictly, the condition is that it has no improper rotation axis.

faq.q: How are enantiomers told apart?
faq.a: By measuring the direction in which they rotate polarized light with a polarimeter, or by using interactions with something chiral, such as chromatography on a chiral stationary phase or NMR with a chiral shift reagent added.

不斉炭素.desc: An sp³ carbon bonded to four different atoms or groups, also called a chiral center. A molecule with exactly one such carbon is always chiral.

エナンチオマー.desc: Stereoisomers that are mirror images of each other and cannot be superimposed. Their physical properties in an achiral environment are identical, and they rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions.

ジアステレオマー.desc: Stereoisomers that are not mirror images. They include isomers differing in configuration at only some stereocenters and cis–trans isomers, and their properties, such as melting point and solubility, differ.

メソ体.desc: A compound with two or more asymmetric carbons that is nonetheless achiral, because an internal mirror plane or similar makes it superimposable on its mirror image. It is not optically active. Example: (2R,3S)-tartaric acid.

CIP順位則.desc: Rules for ranking the substituents on a stereocenter. The higher the atomic number of the directly attached atom, the higher the priority; if tied, the next atoms are compared. Used for R/S and E/Z descriptors.

鏡像体過剰率.desc: A measure of the purity of a mixture of enantiomers, abbreviated ee: the proportion of the major enantiomer minus that of the minor one. 90% R and 10% S gives an ee of 80%.

比旋光度.desc: The observed rotation divided by the path length (dm) and the concentration (g/mL): [α] = α/(l·c). It is characteristic of a substance but changes with temperature, wavelength and solvent.

いす形配座.desc: The most stable conformation of cyclohexane. Its bond angles are nearly tetrahedral and all its bonds are staggered. Each carbon has an axial and an equatorial bond.

SN2反応.desc: A nucleophilic substitution in which the nucleophile attacks carbon from the side opposite the leaving group, with bond formation and bond breaking in a single step. The rate is proportional to the concentrations of both substrate and nucleophile, and it goes with inversion of configuration.

about.p: The SN2 reaction (bimolecular nucleophilic substitution) is a reaction in which the nucleophile attacks carbon from exactly the opposite side of the leaving group, and the formation of the new bond and the breaking of the old one proceed simultaneously in a single step. In the transition state, the three substituents on the central carbon lie nearly in a plane, and the nucleophile and leaving group are partially bonded from either side in a five-coordinate arrangement. There is no intermediate and only one energy barrier. The rate law is v = k[substrate][nucleophile], first order in each and second order overall.

Because the nucleophile attacks from the back, the configuration of the reacting carbon turns inside out like an umbrella in the wind (Walden inversion). From an optically active secondary alkyl halide, a product with inverted configuration is obtained almost exclusively. However, because R/S labels are determined by substituent priorities, if the leaving group and the nucleophile occupy different places in the priority order, the label may not change despite inversion. Whether inversion occurred must be checked from the spatial arrangement, not from the label.

SN2 slows down when the back of the carbon is crowded, so substrate reactivity runs methyl > primary > secondary ≫ tertiary, and tertiary substrates hardly react. Neopentyl-type substrates, branched at the β position, are also very slow. Stronger nucleophiles are favorable, as are leaving groups that are weak bases, such as I⁻, Br⁻ and TsO⁻. Polar aprotic solvents such as DMSO, DMF and acetone, which do not wrap anionic nucleophiles in hydrogen bonds, are particularly suitable.

faq.q: What do the S, N and 2 in SN2 stand for?
faq.a: S stands for substitution and N for nucleophilic, and 2 indicates that it is a bimolecular reaction in which two molecules, the substrate and the nucleophile, take part in the rate-determining step.

faq.q: How do you tell SN2 from SN1?
faq.a: Judge by the substrate class, the strength of the nucleophile and the solvent. A primary substrate, a strong nucleophile and an aprotic solvent favor SN2; a tertiary substrate, a weak nucleophile and a protic solvent favor SN1. In stereochemistry, inversion is the sign of SN2 and racemization the sign of SN1.

faq.q: Why don't tertiary alkyl halides undergo SN2?
faq.a: Because the central carbon carries three alkyl groups and there is no room for the nucleophile to approach from the back. Instead, SN1 or E1 through a carbocation, or E2 if a strong base is present, takes place.

E2反応.desc: A single-step elimination in which a base removes a β-hydrogen as the leaving group departs, forming a double bond. The rate is proportional to the concentrations of substrate and base, and it is fastest in the antiperiplanar arrangement.

about.p: The E2 reaction (bimolecular elimination) is a single-step reaction in which a base removes a hydrogen from the β carbon as a proton while the leaving group departs from the α carbon at the same time, forming a C=C double bond. The rate law is v = k[substrate][base], first order in both the substrate and the base. It does not go through a carbocation, so no rearrangement occurs. Because it proceeds rapidly even with tertiary halides when a strong base is present, alkenes can be obtained efficiently even from crowded substrates that do not undergo SN2.

E2 is fastest in the antiperiplanar arrangement, in which the C−H bond being broken and the C−X bond being cleaved lie in the same plane pointing in opposite directions (a 180° dihedral angle). Because of this stereochemical requirement, diastereomers can give alkenes of different E/Z geometry. On a cyclohexane ring, E2 occurs poorly unless the leaving group and the β-hydrogen are both axial (trans-diaxial), and the reaction is very slow for substrates whose leaving group is locked equatorial.

When there are β-hydrogens at several positions, a small base such as ethoxide gives the more substituted, more stable alkene as the major product (Zaitsev's rule). With a bulky base such as tert-butoxide, the sterically accessible outer hydrogens are removed and the less substituted alkene becomes the major product (the Hofmann product). Elimination from quaternary ammonium salts (Hofmann elimination) also gives mainly the less substituted alkene. The choice of base and leaving group lets you change the product ratio.

faq.q: What is the difference between E2 and E1?
faq.a: E2 is a single-step reaction with a base, and its rate also depends on the base concentration. E1 is a two-step reaction in which the leaving group first departs to form a carbocation and a proton is then lost; its rate depends only on the substrate concentration, and it can involve rearrangements.

faq.q: Which happens, E2 or SN2?
faq.a: Strong, bulky bases, crowded substrates and high temperatures favor E2. With a primary substrate and a good nucleophile of low basicity (I⁻, CN⁻, N3⁻ and the like), SN2 dominates.

faq.q: Does Zaitsev's rule always hold?
faq.a: No. With bulky bases, poor leaving groups such as fluoride, or cyclic substrates that cannot adopt an antiperiplanar arrangement, the less substituted alkene may be formed predominantly.

カルボカチオン.desc: A cation containing a positively charged three-coordinate carbon. It is trigonal planar with an empty p orbital. Stability runs tertiary > secondary > primary, and it is the intermediate in SN1, E1 and addition reactions.

about.p: A carbocation is a cation containing a positively charged three-coordinate carbon; the positive carbon is sp² hybridized and trigonal planar, with one empty p orbital. Stability runs tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl, which is explained by hyperconjugation, the flow of electrons from neighboring C−H and C−C bonds into the empty p orbital, and by the inductive effect of alkyl groups. Allylic and benzylic cations are especially stable because the positive charge is delocalized by resonance, and they undergo SN1 readily even when primary.

SN1, E1, the addition of hydrogen halides to alkenes, and the acid-catalyzed hydration of alkenes and dehydration of alcohols proceed through carbocation intermediates. The step that forms the carbocation is often rate-determining, and the pathway that gives the more stable carbocation is preferred. Markovnikov's rule can also be explained by addition through the more stable carbocation being dominant. Because the intermediate is planar, the nucleophile can attack from either face, and stereocenters tend to racemize.

If the carbon next to a carbocation carries a hydrogen or alkyl group whose migration would give a more stable carbocation, a 1,2-hydride shift or 1,2-alkyl shift occurs rapidly. For example, treating 3-methyl-2-butanol with HBr rearranges the secondary carbocation to a tertiary one, giving mainly 2-bromo-2-methylbutane. In reactions through carbocations, keep in mind that the carbon skeleton and the position of functional groups in the product can differ from those of the starting material.

faq.q: What is the difference between a carbocation and a carbanion?
faq.a: A carbocation is a carbon with a positive charge and an empty p orbital, an electrophilic species that accepts electrons. A carbanion is a carbon with a negative charge and a lone pair, which acts as a nucleophile or base.

faq.q: Why are tertiary carbocations stable?
faq.a: Because hyperconjugation, in which electrons of the alkyl groups' C−H and C−C bonds partly flow into the empty p orbital of the positive carbon, and the inductive effect spread out the positive charge. The more alkyl groups, the greater the stabilization.

faq.q: When do rearrangements occur?
faq.a: They tend to occur when the migration of a hydrogen or alkyl group can give a more stable carbocation, such as secondary to tertiary. Watch for them in reactions through carbocations, such as SN1, E1 and reactions of alcohols under acidic conditions.

SN1反応.desc: A two-step nucleophilic substitution whose rate-determining step is the departure of the leaving group to form a carbocation. The rate is proportional only to the substrate concentration; it occurs readily with tertiary substrates and is accompanied by racemization.

E1反応.desc: A two-step elimination that proceeds through a carbocation. It shares its intermediate with SN1, so the two compete. It is favored by heating and can involve carbocation rearrangements.

脱離基.desc: An atom or group that departs from the substrate with an electron pair in substitution and elimination reactions. The weaker the base, the better the leaving group; examples are I⁻, Br⁻ and TsO⁻. OH⁻ leaves poorly.

ザイツェフ則.desc: The empirical rule that elimination gives as the major product the more stable alkene, with more alkyl groups on the double-bond carbons. It may not hold when a bulky base is used.

マルコフニコフ則.desc: The rule that when HX or a similar reagent adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen atom goes to the carbon that already has more hydrogens. It is explained by the reaction passing through the more stable carbocation.

ヒドロホウ素化.desc: A reaction in which the B−H bond of borane adds syn to an alkene. Subsequent oxidation with basic hydrogen peroxide gives the anti-Markovnikov alcohol with retention of configuration.

芳香族求電子置換反応.desc: A reaction in which a hydrogen on a benzene ring is replaced by an electrophile, such as nitration, halogenation, sulfonation and the Friedel–Crafts reactions. It proceeds through a σ complex.

配向性.desc: The property that decides where a new substituent enters in electrophilic substitution of a substituted benzene. Methyl and OH groups are ortho/para-directing, and nitro and carbonyl groups are meta-directing.

グリニャール試薬.desc: An organomagnesium compound, RMgX, made from an alkyl halide and magnesium in dry ether. It is a strong nucleophile and base, and it reacts with carbonyl compounds to give alcohols.

アルドール反応.desc: A reaction in which an enolate adds as a nucleophile to another carbonyl compound, giving a β-hydroxy carbonyl compound. On heating it dehydrates to an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compound.

けん化.desc: Hydrolysis of an ester with a base such as sodium hydroxide to give a carboxylate salt and an alcohol. The carboxylate formed does not undergo the reverse reaction, so it goes almost to completion.

ランベルト・ベールの法則.desc: The law that the absorbance A is proportional to the concentration c of the absorbing substance and the path length l: A = εcl, where ε is the molar absorptivity. It is the basis of quantitation by UV-Vis absorption spectrophotometry.

about.p: The Beer–Lambert law states that the absorbance A is proportional to the molar concentration c of the absorbing substance and the path length l, written A = εcl. The proportionality constant ε is the molar absorptivity, set by the substance, the wavelength and the solvent. Absorbance is defined as A = −log T = log(I₀/I) and is found from the incident intensity I₀ and the transmitted intensity I. Transmittance T falls exponentially with concentration, so absorbance, which is proportional to concentration, is used for quantitation. A transmittance of 10% corresponds to an absorbance of 1.0, and 1% to 2.0.

The basic approach is to measure the absorbance of standards of known concentration to make a calibration curve and then find the concentration from the sample's absorbance. If ε is known, you can also calculate directly with c = A/(εl). For example, for a compound with ε = 1.5×10⁴ L/(mol·cm), A = 0.45 in a cell with a 1.00 cm path length gives c = 3.0×10⁻⁵ mol/L. If the absorbance is too high, the transmitted light becomes weak and errors grow, so you bring it into a convenient range by diluting or using a cell with a shorter path, then multiply by the factor to recover the original value.

At high concentrations, interactions and aggregation between molecules and changes in refractive index make absorbance no longer proportional to concentration. Other causes of deviation from linearity are light from the monochromator that is not perfectly monochromatic, stray light, scattering from turbid samples, fluorescence of the sample, and chemical equilibria such as dissociation and complexation that change the concentration of the absorbing species. When several components absorb at the same wavelength, the additivity of absorbance (the total is the sum of the components) is used: measuring at several wavelengths and solving simultaneous equations gives each component's concentration.

faq.q: What are the units of molar absorptivity?
faq.a: With concentration in mol/L and path length in cm, ε has units of L/(mol·cm). Absorbance A is dimensionless.

faq.q: How do you convert between transmittance and absorbance?
faq.a: A = −log T. A transmittance of 10% gives A = 1.0, 1% gives A = 2.0, and 50% gives A ≈ 0.30.

faq.q: Why use absorbance rather than transmittance?
faq.a: Because absorbance is proportional to concentration and path length, the calibration curve is a straight line and calculations are easy. Transmittance changes exponentially with concentration.

波数.desc: The number of waves per centimeter, the reciprocal of the wavelength (unit cm⁻¹). It is proportional to energy. IR mainly covers 4000–400 cm⁻¹. λ (µm) = 10000/wavenumber.

吸光度.desc: A quantity expressing how strongly a sample absorbs light: A = −log T = log(I₀/I). A transmittance of 10% gives A = 1.0. It is proportional to concentration and path length, so it is used for quantitation.

モル吸光係数.desc: The proportionality constant ε in the Beer–Lambert law, A = εcl, in L/(mol·cm). It depends on the substance, wavelength and solvent; the larger it is, the more strongly even a small amount absorbs.

蛍光量子収率.desc: The ratio of the number of photons emitted as fluorescence to the number of photons a molecule absorbs, a value between 0 and 1. It is often determined by the relative method, comparing with a reference of known quantum yield.

ストークスシフト.desc: The difference between the maximum of the absorption (excitation) spectrum and the maximum of the fluorescence spectrum. Because part of the energy is lost by vibrational relaxation and the like in the excited state, fluorescence appears on the long-wavelength side.

化学シフト.desc: In NMR, the shift in resonance position caused by differences in shielding by the electrons around a nucleus. It is expressed in ppm relative to TMS (δ 0) and is larger near highly electronegative atoms.

about.p: In NMR, the electrons around a nucleus slightly cancel (shield) the external magnetic field, so even nuclei of the same kind have slightly different resonance frequencies depending on their chemical environment. The chemical shift δ expresses this difference as the offset from the reference compound tetramethylsilane (TMS), in Hz, divided by the spectrometer frequency in MHz; its unit is ppm. Expressed in ppm, the value is the same regardless of the field strength of the instrument; for example, an offset of 2920 Hz on a 400 MHz instrument is δ 7.30.

Rough ¹H NMR values are δ 0.9–1.7 for alkane C−H, 2–2.7 for C−H next to a carbonyl or benzene ring, 3.3–4.5 for C−H on carbons bearing oxygen or halogen, 4.5–6.5 for alkene C−H, 6.5–8.5 for aromatic C−H, 9–10 for aldehydes and 10–13 for carboxylic acid O−H. The closer a highly electronegative atom, the weaker the shielding and the larger δ becomes (further downfield). When several electron-withdrawing groups act together, their effects roughly add up.

The π electrons of benzene rings, C=O and C=C set up ring currents and the like in a magnetic field, strengthening or weakening the field depending on location (magnetic anisotropy). This is why aromatic and aldehyde protons appear especially far downfield. ¹³C NMR chemical shifts span a wide range, about 0–220 ppm: sp³ carbons appear at 0–90, aromatic and alkene carbons at 100–160 and carbonyl carbons around 160–220 ppm. Because the range is so wide, signals rarely overlap in ¹³C spectra.

faq.q: What do downfield and upfield mean?
faq.a: The side with larger δ (the left of the spectrum) is called downfield, and the side with smaller δ (the right) upfield. The less shielded a proton, the further downfield it appears.

faq.q: Why is it expressed in ppm?
faq.a: Because the offset in resonance frequency (Hz) is proportional to the field strength of the instrument, dividing by the spectrometer frequency to get ppm gives values that can be compared on any instrument.

faq.q: Why does the position of O−H and N−H signals vary?
faq.a: Because the extent of hydrogen bonding changes with concentration, solvent and temperature, and proton exchange also occurs. Adding D2O exchanges H for D and makes the signal disappear, which is useful for confirming assignments.

スピン結合.desc: The phenomenon in which nearby nonequivalent nuclei split each other's signals through the bonding electrons. With n equivalent protons next door, a signal splits into n+1 lines.

about.p: Spin–spin coupling is the phenomenon in which nearby magnetically nonequivalent nuclei slightly change the field each other feels through the bonding electrons. Depending on whether the spin of a neighboring proton is aligned with or against the field, the resonance frequency of the observed proton shifts slightly, so its signal splits into several lines. The spacing of the splitting is called the coupling constant J and is expressed in Hz. J is determined by molecular structure and is independent of the instrument's field strength, so it provides structural clues.

With n equivalent protons on the neighboring carbon, a signal splits into n + 1 lines, with intensities following Pascal's triangle (doublet 1:1, triplet 1:2:1, quartet 1:3:3:1). In an ethyl group, the CH3 becomes a triplet from the neighboring CH2 and the CH2 a quartet from the neighboring CH3, a combination that marks an ethyl group. In an isopropyl group, the two CH3 groups are a doublet and the CH a septet. Chemically equivalent protons do not split each other.

The size of J reflects the number of bonds between the nuclei and their angles. Coupling between protons on adjacent carbons (³J) is usually about 6–8 Hz, but in alkenes the trans arrangement gives about 12–18 Hz and the cis arrangement about 6–12 Hz, a difference used to assign E/Z geometry. In cyclohexanes, the coupling between two axial protons is large, about 8–13 Hz, which helps assign conformations. Coupling to several kinds of protons with different coupling constants gives patterns such as a doublet of doublets rather than the simple n + 1 form.

faq.q: When can the n+1 rule be used?
faq.a: When all the neighboring protons couple with nearly the same J. Coupling to two kinds of protons (n and m of them) with different coupling constants gives up to (n+1)(m+1) lines.

faq.q: Why is an OH proton often not split?
faq.a: In many solvents the OH proton exchanges rapidly between molecules, so its coupling to neighboring protons is averaged away and it appears as a broad singlet.

faq.q: Does the coupling constant J change with the instrument?
faq.a: No. The difference in chemical shift expressed in Hz, on the other hand, grows in proportion to the spectrometer frequency, so multiplets overlap less on higher-field instruments.

分子イオンピーク.desc: In a mass spectrum, the peak due to the radical cation M⁺· formed when one electron is removed from the molecule. Its m/z gives the molecular weight. It is not necessarily the base peak.

about.p: In electron ionization (EI) mass spectrometry, vaporized molecules are hit with electrons of about 70 eV, knocking one electron out of the molecule to form the radical cation M⁺·. This is called the molecular ion, and its m/z equals the nominal molecular weight calculated with the most abundant isotopes. The molecular-ion peak tells you the compound's molecular weight directly and is the first peak to check in structure determination. It is not necessarily the most intense peak (the base peak), however, and for compounds that fragment easily it may be almost invisible.

Just to the right of the molecular ion appear small peaks from molecules containing heavier isotopes. The natural abundance of ¹³C is about 1.1%, so for a molecule with n carbons the M+1 peak is roughly 1.1n% of M. Chlorine occurs as ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl in about a 3:1 ratio and bromine as ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br in about 1:1, so molecules containing one of these show characteristic pairs of peaks, M:M+2 ≈ 3:1 and 1:1 respectively, which help determine whether halogens are present and how many.

about.h: The nitrogen rule and soft ionization
about.p: For molecules made of C, H, N, O and similar elements, an odd number of nitrogens gives an odd molecular weight, and zero or an even number gives an even one (the nitrogen rule). When the molecular ion is too weak to give the molecular weight, soft ionization such as chemical ionization (CI) or electrospray ionization (ESI) is used, and the molecular weight is found from the protonated molecule [M+H]⁺ or the sodium adduct [M+Na]⁺. Measuring the accurate mass by high-resolution MS can then narrow things down to the molecular formula.

faq.q: Are the molecular-ion peak and the base peak the same?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The base peak is the most intense peak in the spectrum and is often a stable fragment ion. In neopentane, for example, m/z 57 is the base peak, and the molecular ion (m/z 72) is barely visible.

faq.q: How do you recognize the molecular-ion peak?
faq.a: Check that it is on the highest-m/z side of the spectrum, that there are no neighboring peaks at chemically impossible mass differences such as 3–14 below it, and that it is consistent with the nitrogen rule and isotope patterns.

faq.q: Are the peaks in an ESI spectrum also molecular ions?
faq.a: In ESI, mainly [M+H]⁺, [M−H]⁻ and adduct ions are observed, which strictly are not radical-cation molecular ions. Subtract the mass of the added ion from the m/z to find the molecular weight.

窒素ルール.desc: The rule that for molecules made of C, H, N, O and similar elements, an odd number of nitrogen atoms gives an odd molecular weight, and zero or an even number gives an even one. Used in interpreting molecular ions.

マクラファティ転位.desc: A rearrangement in mass spectrometry in which a γ-hydrogen moves to the carbonyl oxygen, the α–β bond breaks and a neutral alkene is lost. 2-Hexanone gives an ion at m/z 58.

同位体ピーク.desc: A peak due to molecules containing heavier isotopes. One chlorine gives M:M+2 ≈ 3:1 and one bromine about 1:1, which is used to judge whether halogens are present and how many.

高分解能質量分析.desc: Mass spectrometry that measures ion masses to about four decimal places. It distinguishes species with the same nominal mass, such as CO, N2 and C2H4, and fixes the molecular formula from the accurate mass.

理論段数.desc: A number expressing the separation efficiency of a chromatographic column, found as N = 16(tR/W)² or 5.54(tR/W½)². The larger it is, the sharper the peaks. Resolution is proportional to √N.

about.p: The theoretical plate number N is a number expressing the separation efficiency of a chromatographic column, borrowed from the analogy of the plates in a distillation column. It shows how much a component's band spreads as it travels through the column, and for a Gaussian peak it is N = (tR/σ)². In practice it is found from the baseline width W of the peak as N = 16(tR/W)², or from the width at half height W½ as N = 5.54(tR/W½)². For example, a retention time of 10.0 min and a baseline width of 0.40 min give N = 10000 plates. The larger N, the sharper the peak at the same retention time.

The column length L divided by the plate number, H = L/N, is called the plate height (HETP) and represents the length per plate. The smaller H, the more efficient the column, and it allows columns of different lengths to be compared. In HPLC, smaller packing particles give smaller H; for example, a 150 mm column with N = 13850 plates has H ≈ 11 µm. H changes with the mobile-phase flow velocity, a relationship described by the van Deemter equation, and there is an optimum flow velocity at which H is smallest.

The resolution Rs, which expresses how well two peaks are separated, is determined by the square root of the plate number, the separation factor α and the retention factor k, as Rs = (√N/4)·((α − 1)/α)·(k/(1 + k)). Quadrupling N only doubles Rs, so to improve a separation it is often more effective to increase α by changing the mobile or stationary phase. When peak shapes depart from Gaussian (tailing and so on), the plate number depends on how it is calculated, so compare values obtained by the same method.

faq.q: How is the plate number calculated?
faq.a: From the retention time and peak width, with N = 16(tR/W)² (baseline width) or N = 5.54(tR/W½)² (width at half height). Express the retention time and width in the same units.

faq.q: Does the plate number differ between components?
faq.a: Yes. Even on the same column, the value changes with a component's diffusion coefficient and retention factor and with the flow rate. Column performance specifications use values for designated test compounds and conditions.

faq.q: How can the plate number be increased?
faq.a: Use packings with smaller particles, lengthen the column, bring the flow rate close to its optimum, and reduce the volume of extra-column tubing and the detector cell.

保持係数.desc: k = (tR − t0)/t0, the ratio of the time a component spends in the stationary phase to the time it spends in the mobile phase. Also called the capacity factor. It does not depend on column length or flow rate.

分離係数.desc: The ratio of the retention factors of two components, α = k2/k1 (with the later-eluting component in the numerator). It expresses the selectivity of the stationary and mobile phases; at α = 1 no increase in plate number will separate them.

分離度.desc: The degree of separation of two adjacent peaks, Rs = 2(tR2 − tR1)/(W1 + W2). Rs of about 1.5 gives nearly baseline separation. It is proportional to the square root of the plate number.

逆相クロマトグラフィー.desc: Liquid chromatography using a nonpolar stationary phase such as ODS (C18) and a polar mobile phase such as water–methanol. The more hydrophobic a component, the later it elutes.

水素炎イオン化検出器.desc: A GC detector, abbreviated FID, that measures as a current the ions produced when organic compounds burn in a hydrogen flame. It is highly sensitive to hydrocarbons and barely responds to water, CO2 or permanent gases.

内部標準法.desc: A quantitation method in which a fixed amount of an internal standard is added to the samples and standards, and the analyte is quantified from its peak-area ratio to the internal standard. It cancels variations in injection volume and losses during sample preparation.

ネルンスト式.desc: The relation between electrode potential and activity, E = E° + (2.303RT/nF) log(oxidized/reduced). At 25 °C for a one-electron reaction, the potential changes by about 59.2 mV per tenfold change in activity.

ガラス電極.desc: A pH electrode that uses the membrane potential created by the difference in hydrogen-ion activity across a thin glass membrane. Ideally it changes by about 59.2 mV per pH unit at 25 °C, and it is calibrated with two or more standard buffers.

電位差滴定.desc: A titration in which the potential difference between an indicator electrode and a reference electrode is measured, and the equivalence point is found where the potential changes most steeply. End points can be found even in colored or turbid samples.

原子吸光分析.desc: A method in which the sample is atomized in a flame or graphite furnace, and the concentration is found from how much light of the wavelength characteristic of the target element is absorbed by ground-state atoms. A hollow cathode lamp is used as the light source.

ICP質量分析.desc: A method, abbreviated ICP-MS, that measures elements ionized in an inductively coupled plasma with a mass spectrometer. It can measure ultratrace elements and isotope ratios, but watch out for polyatomic interferences.

検出限界.desc: The smallest amount or concentration at which a component can be judged to be present, distinguishable from the blank. Three times the standard deviation σ of the blank divided by the slope of the calibration curve (3σ/slope) is widely used.

検量線.desc: A line, obtained by measuring standards of known concentration, that relates concentration to the measured value (absorbance, peak area and so on). It is used to find concentrations from sample readings. Avoid extrapolating beyond its range.

有効数字.desc: The reliable digits of a measured value plus the last, uncertain digit. In addition and subtraction, match the value with the fewest decimal places; in multiplication and division, the value with the fewest significant figures.

当量点.desc: The point in a titration at which the amount of standard solution added has reacted exactly with the analyte according to the reaction equation. Strictly, it is distinguished from the end point, where the indicator changes color.

about.p: The equivalence point is the theoretical point at which the substance in the sample and the added standard solution have reacted exactly, in the proportions of the reaction equation. The end point, by contrast, is the point taken as the equivalence point in an actual experiment, such as a change in indicator color or a sudden change in potential. If the indicator's transition range is offset from the equivalence point, the difference between end point and equivalence point becomes the titration error. Choosing the right indicator is nothing other than bringing the end point as close as possible to the equivalence point. In standardization, which fixes the concentration of the standard solution, titrating with the same indicator and conditions also helps errors cancel.

about.h: The equivalence-point pH depends on acid and base strength
about.p: At the equivalence point of an acid–base titration, the solution is an aqueous solution of the salt formed. For a strong acid with a strong base (HCl and NaOH), the salt does not hydrolyze, so the pH is about 7 at 25 °C. When a weak acid is titrated with a strong base, the conjugate base (such as acetate) hydrolyzes to produce OH⁻, so the pH is on the basic side, about 8.7 for 0.05 mol/L sodium acetate. When a weak base is titrated with a strong acid, the conjugate acid (NH4⁺) releases H⁺, giving the acidic side, about 5.3. The equivalence-point pH can be calculated from the salt concentration and Kb = Kw/Ka.

about.h: Titration curve shape and the pH jump
about.p: A titration curve plots pH against the volume added. Near the equivalence point a pH jump appears, in which a tiny volume changes the pH greatly, and it is larger the higher the concentration and the stronger the acid or base. In the titration of a weak acid, the region before the equivalence point is a buffer where the pH changes gradually, and at the half-neutralization point pH = pKa. If the acid is too weak or too dilute, the pH jump becomes indistinct and the end point is hard to find with an indicator, so the equivalence point is found by potentiometric titration from the maximum of the derivative curve.

faq.q: Are the end point and the equivalence point the same thing?
faq.a: No. The equivalence point is a theoretical point set by the reaction equation, and the end point is the point actually observed, such as an indicator color change. The difference between them is the titration error, so choose an indicator whose transition range falls near the equivalence point.

faq.q: Is the pH at the equivalence point always 7?
faq.a: It is 7 only for a strong acid with a strong base. Titrating a weak acid with a strong base gives the basic side, and titrating a weak base with a strong acid gives the acidic side.

faq.q: How many equivalence points does a polyprotic acid have?
faq.a: If the pKa values of the steps are far enough apart, an equivalence point appears for each step. Titrating sodium carbonate with hydrochloric acid shows two end points, at about pH 8.3 and about pH 4, which the Warder method makes use of.

pH指示薬.desc: A weak-acid or weak-base dye whose color changes with the pH of the solution. Choose one whose transition range falls within the steep pH change near the equivalence point. Phenolphthalein and methyl orange are typical examples.

一次標準物質.desc: A substance that is highly pure, stable without absorbing moisture or decomposing, and can be weighed accurately. It serves as the reference for fixing the concentration of standard solutions. Examples include potassium hydrogen phthalate, sodium carbonate and sodium oxalate.

標定.desc: The operation of determining the exact concentration of a standard solution by titration against a primary standard or similar. Sodium hydroxide and potassium permanganate solutions must always be standardized after preparation before use.

キレート滴定.desc: Titration based on complex formation between a chelating agent such as EDTA and metal ions. EDTA binds metals 1 : 1 regardless of their charge and is used to determine water hardness and metal ions.

about.p: Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) is a hexadentate ligand that coordinates to a metal ion at six sites: two nitrogens and the oxygens of four carboxy groups. A single molecule wraps around the metal ion and forms several five-membered chelate rings, giving complexes far more stable than those of monodentate ligands. As a result, it almost always forms 1 : 1 complexes even with metals of different charge, such as Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺ and Fe³⁺. A major advantage in titration calculations is that the moles of EDTA added can be taken directly as the moles of metal ion.

about.h: pH and the conditional formation constant
about.p: EDTA is an acid that dissociates in four steps, and the form that binds metals strongly is fully deprotonated Y⁴⁻. At low pH the fraction of Y⁴⁻ becomes small, and the conditional formation constant, the apparent stability including the effect of pH, decreases. Fe³⁺, whose complex is very stable, can be titrated even in acid at pH 1–2, but Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ do not give a clear end point unless the pH is around 10. On the other hand, raising the pH too far precipitates metal hydroxides, so it is important to hold the pH that suits the purpose with a buffer. These pH differences can also be used to determine coexisting metals separately.

The end point of a complexometric titration is detected with a metal indicator that changes color when it forms a complex with the metal. Eriochrome Black T (EBT) at pH 10 is red when complexed with Mg²⁺ and the like and blue when free. As EDTA is added, the metal transfers from the indicator to EDTA, and when it has all transferred the color turns blue. Water hardness is often expressed in mg/L as the total Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ converted to the mass of CaCO3, and Ca²⁺ alone can be found by precipitating Mg(OH)2 at pH 12–13 and titrating with NN indicator (calconcarboxylic acid).

faq.q: Do you need to consider the metal's charge in EDTA titrations?
faq.a: Not for the mole ratio. EDTA forms complexes almost 1 : 1 regardless of charge, so you can set moles of EDTA = moles of metal ion.

faq.q: Why is a buffer added?
faq.a: Because the strength of binding between EDTA and the metal changes greatly with pH, and complex formation also releases H⁺. Holding the pH constant with a buffer keeps the conditional formation constant large enough and makes the indicator color change sharp.

faq.q: What is used to standardize an EDTA standard solution?
faq.a: Solutions of high-purity zinc or calcium carbonate dissolved in acid are commonly used. Titrating with the same indicator and pH as the samples helps errors cancel.

溶解度積.desc: The constant Ksp obtained by multiplying the ion concentrations, each raised to the power of its coefficient, in a saturated solution of a sparingly soluble salt; for AgCl, [Ag⁺][Cl⁻]. Solubilities of salts with different formula types cannot be compared by the size of Ksp.

モール法.desc: A precipitation titration of chloride ion with silver nitrate using potassium chromate as the indicator. The end point is signaled by reddish-brown Ag2CrO4 forming after AgCl, and it is carried out in neutral to weakly basic solution.

ヨウ素滴定.desc: Titration based on the redox chemistry of iodine. I2 liberated by an oxidizing agent is titrated with sodium thiosulfate, and starch is added near the end point. Used to determine copper, dissolved oxygen and chlorine.

逆合成解析.desc: A way of planning syntheses that starts from the target molecule and hypothetically disconnects bonds that known reactions can form, working back to readily available precursors. It is written with the arrow "⇒".

about.p: Retrosynthetic analysis is a method of synthesis planning systematized by E. J. Corey. Instead of thinking forward from the starting materials, you start from the target molecule and ask which bond, if formed last, would split it into simpler precursors. One retrosynthetic step is written with the arrow "⇒", and this is repeated until readily available starting materials are reached. A single molecule can be disconnected in many ways, so several routes are drawn and compared, and the best one is chosen on the basis of the number of steps, yield, availability of starting materials, safety and so on.

Hypothetically cutting a bond is called a disconnection, and the idealized fragments it produces are called synthons. Synthons take forms such as C⁻ and C⁺ and often do not exist as such, so they are replaced by reagents actually used (synthetic equivalents). For example, disconnecting the C−C bond next to a carbonyl group, the nucleophilic carbon synthon corresponds to a Grignard reagent or an enolate, and the electrophilic carbon synthon to an aldehyde or ketone. The principle is to disconnect at positions that correspond to the reverse of reactions known to proceed reliably.

A C−C bond joining two aromatic rings is easiest to think of as disconnected in correspondence with the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling (aryl halide + boronic acid). Reversing a C=C double bond to a Wittig reaction (carbonyl compound + phosphorus ylide) fixes the position of the double bond reliably. A cyclohexene ring can be split by the Diels–Alder reaction into a diene and a dienophile, and esters and amides are split into carboxylic acid derivatives and alcohols or amines. Functional group interconversion (FGI), converting one functional group into another to make a disconnection easier, is also a common move.

The overall yield of a linear multistep synthesis is the product of the step yields, so even at 80% per step it falls to about 41% after four steps and about 11% after ten. Retrosynthesis therefore favors fewer steps and disconnections that split the molecule into large fragments near its middle. A convergent synthesis, in which two or more fragments are made separately and joined at the end, shortens the longest linear sequence and makes a higher overall yield easier to achieve. When there are functional groups that should not react, the protection and deprotection steps are also counted when comparing routes.

faq.q: How does retrosynthetic analysis differ from predicting reactions?
faq.a: Predicting reactions is forward thinking, from starting materials to products; retrosynthetic analysis is backward thinking, from the target molecule to starting materials. In synthesis planning, routes are devised by retrosynthesis and each step is then checked as a forward reaction.

faq.q: What is a synthon?
faq.a: An idealized fragment produced when a bond is disconnected in retrosynthesis. It often does not exist in that form, and in practice a reagent that plays the same role (a synthetic equivalent), such as a Grignard reagent or an aldehyde, is used.

faq.q: What makes a good synthetic route?
faq.a: Few steps and a high overall yield, starting materials that are available and safe, and little by-product and waste (atom economy). Routes with fewer protecting-group installations and removals are generally favored.

保護基.desc: A group that temporarily converts a functional group that should not react into another form to protect it. Examples are acetals for ketones, TBS ethers for alcohols and the Boc group for amines; it is removed after the reaction.

鈴木・宮浦カップリング.desc: A reaction that forms C−C bonds from aryl halides and organoboron compounds in the presence of a palladium catalyst and a base. It is widely used to make biaryls, and the boron reagents are stable and of low toxicity.

about.p: The Suzuki–Miyaura coupling reacts an aryl halide or aryl triflate, Ar−X, with an organoboron compound such as a boronic acid, Ar'B(OH)2, or a boronic ester, in the presence of a palladium catalyst and a base, to make Ar−Ar'. Biaryl structures, with two aromatic rings joined directly, are common in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals and liquid-crystal materials, and this method has become indispensable for making them. Akira Suzuki shared the 2010 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Heck and Negishi for developing such reactions. It can also join two alkenyl groups or an aryl and an alkenyl group.

The reaction proceeds through three elementary steps. First, Pd(0) inserts into the C−X bond of Ar−X by oxidative addition, giving Ar−Pd(II)−X. Next comes transmetalation, in which Ar' moves to palladium from the organoboron compound, activated by the base as a borate. Finally, reductive elimination releases Ar−Ar' and regenerates Pd(0). Oxidative addition occurs most readily in the order C−I > C−Br > C−Cl, and using inexpensive aryl chlorides requires measures such as electron-rich, bulky phosphine ligands.

about.h: How it differs from other couplings
about.p: The organoboron compounds of the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling are relatively stable to air and water, easy to handle and of low toxicity, and the borate by-products can be washed out with water. It tolerates many functional groups, including carbonyls, esters and nitro groups, and proceeds even in water-containing solvents. The Migita–Kosugi–Stille coupling (usually just called the Stille coupling), using organotin compounds, suffers from toxicity, and the Kumada–Tamao–Corriu coupling (Kumada coupling), using Grignard reagents, from limited functional-group tolerance. The Heck reaction, which joins alkenes and aryl halides, uses no organometallic reagent and differs in leaving a C=C through β-hydride elimination.

faq.q: Why is a base needed?
faq.a: The boron of a boronic acid has low nucleophilicity, so a base is added to convert it into a negatively charged borate, which makes it easier to hand the organic group over to palladium in transmetalation.

faq.q: Which aryl halides react most readily?
faq.a: The ease of oxidative addition runs I > Br > Cl, and iodides and bromides react under mild conditions. Chlorides are inexpensive but often need catalysts with highly active ligands.

faq.q: How much catalyst is used?
faq.a: In the laboratory, a few mol% or less relative to the substrate is typical, and highly active catalysts work at less than 0.1 mol%. The higher the turnover number (TON), the less palladium is used and the less remains in the product.

ヘック反応.desc: A reaction that joins an aryl halide and an alkene in the presence of a palladium catalyst and a base. Through insertion and β-hydride elimination, a substituted alkene (usually the E isomer) is obtained.

ウィッティヒ反応.desc: A reaction that makes alkenes from aldehydes or ketones and a phosphorus ylide, Ph3P=CR2. A C=C forms exactly where the C=O was, and formation of the strong P=O bond is the driving force.

ディールス・アルダー反応.desc: A concerted [4+2] cycloaddition between a diene in the s-cis conformation and a dienophile, forming a cyclohexene ring. It is stereospecific: the configuration of the dienophile is retained in the product.

収率.desc: The amount in moles of product actually obtained as a fraction of the theoretical yield, the amount formed if all of the limiting reagent became product. The overall yield of a multistep synthesis is the product of the step yields.

原子効率.desc: The fraction of reactant atoms incorporated into the desired product, found by dividing the molar mass of the desired product by the total molar mass of the reactants. It is a guide to how much by-product is formed.

付加重合.desc: Polymerization in which monomers link one after another by opening C=C double bonds and the like. No by-product is released, and the repeat unit has the same composition as the monomer. Examples are polyethylene and polystyrene.

縮合重合.desc: Polymerization in which functional groups join while releasing a small molecule such as water. The molecular weight builds up stepwise; nylon 66 and polyesters are typical examples.

ラジカル重合.desc: Chain-growth polymerization in which radicals generated from an initiator add to monomers and proceed through three stages: initiation, propagation and termination. High-molecular-weight polymer forms from the start of the reaction.

about.p: In radical polymerization, an initiator such as AIBN or benzoyl peroxide first decomposes by heat or light to form radicals, which add to the C=C of a monomer in the initiation step. Propagation, in which the next monomer adds to the resulting carbon radical, is repeated hundreds or thousands of times, and the chain is completed by termination, in which two growing radicals meet and their unpaired electrons disappear. Termination occurs by combination, in which the ends of two chains bond, and by disproportionation, in which a hydrogen atom transfers to give two chains.

At steady state, the rates of radical formation and termination balance, and the radical concentration is proportional to the square root of the initiator concentration [I]. The polymerization rate Rp = kp[M][R·] is also proportional to [I]^(1/2), so quadrupling the initiator doubles the rate. On the other hand, the number of monomers a chain adds before terminating (the kinetic chain length) is proportional to [M]/[I]^(1/2), and adding more initiator lowers the molecular weight. That rate and molecular weight move in opposite directions in this way is the basis for setting the conditions of a radical polymerization.

When a growing radical abstracts a hydrogen atom from the solvent, a thiol or the like, that chain stops growing, and the new radical formed starts the next chain. This is called chain transfer; because the number of radicals does not change, the polymerization rate changes little and only the molecular weight falls. Industrially, small amounts of chain-transfer agents such as 1-dodecanethiol are added to control molecular weight. Inhibitors such as hydroquinone, by contrast, trap radicals and stop the polymerization itself, so they are used to prevent monomers from polymerizing during storage.

Radical polymerization proceeds even in the presence of water and many functional groups and works for a wide range of monomers, including styrene, acrylic esters, vinyl chloride and vinyl acetate, making it the most widely used polymerization method in industry. It can be run in bulk, solution, suspension or emulsion, chosen for the purpose. On the other hand, termination cannot be avoided, so the molecular-weight distribution is broad (dispersity of about 1.5–2 or more), and chain lengths and end structures are hard to control. To overcome this, living (controlled) radical polymerizations that suppress termination have been developed.

faq.q: Why is the molecular weight high from the start of a radical polymerization?
faq.a: Because a single initiated radical adds hundreds to thousands of monomers during the short time before it terminates. While conversion is low, the mixture is high-molecular-weight polymer plus unreacted monomer, and it is mainly the yield that increases with time.

faq.q: What happens to the molecular weight if more initiator is used?
faq.a: There are more radicals, which meet each other more readily, so each chain is shorter and the molecular weight falls. In the steady-state approximation, the molecular weight is inversely proportional to the square root of the initiator concentration, and the polymerization rate is proportional to it.

faq.q: Why does oxygen delay polymerization?
faq.a: Oxygen reacts rapidly with growing radicals to form unreactive peroxy radicals, which hinders polymerization. For this reason, dissolved oxygen is usually removed before polymerization, for example by bubbling nitrogen through the mixture.

数平均分子量.desc: The average molecular weight of a polymer obtained by dividing its total mass by the total number of molecules (moles), Mn = ΣNiMi/ΣNi. It is strongly influenced by the numerous low-molecular-weight components.

重量平均分子量.desc: The average molecular weight weighted by the mass of each component, Mw = ΣNiMi²/ΣNiMi. It is strongly influenced by high-molecular-weight components and is always larger than Mn when there is a distribution.

分散度.desc: The ratio Mw/Mn of the weight-average to the number-average molecular weight (symbol Đ). It expresses the breadth of the molecular-weight distribution; it is 1 if all molecules have the same length and is never less than 1.

about.p: When there are Ni molecules of molecular weight Mi, the number-average molecular weight is Mn = ΣNiMi/ΣNi and the weight-average molecular weight is Mw = ΣNiMi²/ΣNiMi. Mn is the total mass divided by the total number of molecules and can be obtained from end-group analysis or osmotic pressure. Mw is the average weighted by the mass of each component and can be obtained from light scattering. For example, mixing 1.0 g each of components with molecular weights 1.0×10⁴ and 3.0×10⁴ gives Mn of 1.5×10⁴ and Mw of 2.0×10⁴, a dispersity of about 1.33.

Dispersity Đ = Mw/Mn is a measure of the breadth of the molecular-weight distribution. If all molecules have the same length, Mw = Mn and Đ = 1, and the broader the distribution, the larger it becomes. It used to be called the polydispersity index (PDI), but the name dispersity and the symbol Đ are now used following IUPAC recommendations. Even at the same Mn, a different dispersity means different melt viscosity, strength and processability, so it is reported together with Mn and Mw as a basic figure describing polymer quality.

The molecular-weight distribution of step-growth polymerization (polycondensation) follows Flory's most probable distribution, with Đ = 1 + p, which approaches 2 as the extent of reaction p approaches 1. In radical polymerization the theoretical values are about 1.5 if termination is only by combination and about 2 if by disproportionation, but in practice the conditions change as conversion rises, and the distribution is often even broader. In living anionic polymerization, with no termination or chain transfer, all chains start almost simultaneously and grow at the same rate, so Đ is close to 1, at 1.1 or below.

The molecular-weight distribution is generally measured by gel permeation chromatography (GPC). Molecules elute in order of their size in solution, largest first, and the molecular weight at each elution volume is found from a calibration curve of log M against elution volume made with standards such as polystyrene. Mn, Mw and Đ are calculated from the distribution obtained in this way. Because the values are equivalents obtained by comparing size with the standards, however, they deviate from the true values for polymers of different shape. Adding a light-scattering detector gives absolute molecular weights that do not rely on standards.

faq.q: Can the dispersity be less than 1?
faq.a: No. Mw is a mass-weighted average, so whenever there is a distribution it is larger than the number average Mn; only when all molecules have the same molecular weight is Mw = Mn and the dispersity 1.

faq.q: Are the polydispersity index (PDI) and dispersity the same thing?
faq.a: Both refer to Mw/Mn. IUPAC now recommends the term dispersity and the symbol Đ.

faq.q: What is the dispersity of a natural protein?
faq.a: A particular protein is synthesized with a defined sequence and length according to genetic information, so a sample of a single kind of molecule has a dispersity of 1. This is a major difference from synthetic polymers.

カロザースの式.desc: The relation between the number-average degree of polymerization of a step-growth polymerization and the extent of reaction p, Xn = 1/(1 − p). Even at p = 0.99, Xn is only 100, showing that high molecular weight requires an extremely high extent of reaction.

ゲル浸透クロマトグラフィー.desc: A method that separates polymers by their size in solution on a column packed with a porous gel. Larger molecules elute first, and the molecular-weight distribution is found by comparison with standards.

熱重量測定.desc: Thermal analysis (TG) that continuously measures the change in a sample's mass while its temperature is varied. Mass losses from dehydration, decomposition and combustion and gains from oxidation reveal composition and thermal stability.

示差走査熱量測定.desc: Thermal analysis (DSC) that measures the difference in heat flow into or out of a sample and a reference. It is used to quantify heats of fusion and reaction and to measure glass transition temperatures and heat capacities.

about.p: DSC heats and cools a sample and a reference (an empty pan, alumina or similar) on the same program and records the difference in heat flow into or out of them. There are power-compensation instruments, which measure the difference in power needed to keep the two at the same temperature, and heat-flux instruments, which convert the temperature difference between the two into heat flow by calibration. If temperature and heat are calibrated with a substance of known melting point and heat of fusion, such as indium, the enthalpy of transitions and reactions can be quantified in J/g from the peak area. Compared with DTA, which measures only the temperature difference, its strength is the quantification of heat.

The glass transition involves no latent heat and is a discontinuous increase in heat capacity, so on a DSC curve the baseline shifts in a step toward the endothermic side, and its midpoint or similar is taken as the glass transition temperature Tg. Melting is a first-order transition with latent heat, so it appears as an endothermic peak whose area is the heat of fusion. Crystallization is an exothermic peak, and heating a quenched polymer above Tg shows the exotherm of cold crystallization. In samples stored for a long time, a small endothermic peak (enthalpy relaxation) overlaps the step at Tg, so take care not to mistake it for melting.

For semicrystalline polymers, the crystallinity is estimated by dividing the heat of fusion by the heat of fusion of the 100% crystalline polymer, ΔH°. When cold crystallization occurs during heating, its exotherm is subtracted from the heat of fusion so that only the crystals present before the measurement are counted. For example, for PET with cold crystallization of 20.0 J/g, melting of 50.0 J/g and ΔH° = 140 J/g, the crystallinity is (50.0 − 20.0)/140 = 21.4%. The value of ΔH° differs slightly between sources, so use the same value when comparing.

The DSC curve of a polymer depends strongly on its temperature history during molding and storage (thermal history). To see the actual state of a product, use the first heating; to compare the materials themselves, use the second heating after melting once and cooling at a constant rate. A higher heating rate increases sensitivity, but peaks shift to higher temperature and broaden, so it is important to match the rate, sample mass, pan and purge gas between samples being compared. If the sample does not sit flat against the bottom of the pan, heat transfer is poor and peaks broaden or shift in temperature, so pay attention to how the sample is packed.

faq.q: How do DSC and DTA differ?
faq.a: DTA measures the temperature difference between the sample and a reference and is used mainly to find the temperatures of transitions and reactions. DSC measures the difference in heat flow, so enthalpies are easier to quantify from peak areas, and changes in heat capacity can also be measured.

faq.q: In DSC, is endothermic or exothermic plotted upward?
faq.a: Depending on the instrument and standard, endotherms are drawn either up or down. Always check the "endo" and "exo" directions marked on the graph's axis before reading it.

faq.q: Is the glass transition temperature a single fixed value?
faq.a: The glass transition is a change spread over a temperature range, and the value shifts by several degrees depending on whether the onset, midpoint or endpoint is taken and on the heating rate. When reporting it, state which point was taken and the measurement conditions.

ガラス転移温度.desc: The temperature Tg at which amorphous regions change from a glassy state to a rubbery state (supercooled liquid). It involves no latent heat and appears in DSC as a step in the baseline.

ブラッグの式.desc: The relation 2d sin θ = nλ between a crystal's interplanar spacing d, the diffraction angle θ and the X-ray wavelength λ. The angle read on a diffractometer is 2θ, so it is halved to use θ in calculations.

粉末X線回折.desc: A method (XRD) that shines X-rays on a powder sample and identifies crystalline phases from the positions and intensities of the diffraction peaks. It distinguishes polymorphs of the same composition, and peak widths also give crystallite sizes.

蛍光X線分析.desc: A method (XRF) that excites a sample with primary X-rays and determines the kinds and amounts of elements from their characteristic X-rays (fluorescent X-rays). It measures many elements nondestructively but struggles with light elements.

X線光電子分光.desc: A method (XPS) that finds binding energies from the kinetic energies of photoelectrons emitted by X-rays, probing the elements and chemical states in the top few nm of a surface. Chemical shifts reveal which atoms an element is bonded to.

about.p: XPS irradiates a sample in ultrahigh vacuum with X-rays such as Al Kα (1486.6 eV) or Mg Kα (1253.6 eV) and measures the kinetic energy EK of the electrons ejected by the photoelectric effect. The binding energy is found as EB = hν − EK − φ (φ is the spectrometer work function). Binding energies are fixed for each element and orbital, so elements are identified from the positions of peaks such as C 1s, O 1s and Fe 2p, and the surface composition is estimated from peak areas corrected with sensitivity factors. Hydrogen and helium cannot be measured.

Even for the same element, the binding energy shifts by several eV depending on what it is bonded to. This is called the chemical shift: the more electrons are pulled away by bonding to highly electronegative atoms, the more tightly the core electrons are bound to the nucleus and the higher the binding energy. For C 1s, roughly, C−C and C−H are at 284.8 eV, C−O at 286.5 eV, O−C=O at 289 eV and CF2 at 292 eV. Metals and their oxides also give different values, so XPS is used to study the extent of surface oxidation and the proportions of functional groups introduced by surface treatment.

Photoelectrons generated inside a sample travel while undergoing inelastic scattering, so only those generated within roughly a few nm of the surface can escape without losing energy. The information depth of XPS is therefore a few nm, giving information entirely different from SEM-EDS, which includes depths of about a µm, or X-ray fluorescence, which measures even deeper regions. Changes in composition deeper down are examined by depth profiling, measuring while gradually sputtering away the surface with argon ions, although sputtering can change the chemical state.

In insulating samples, the surface charges positively by the amount of photoelectrons lost, shifting all peaks toward higher binding energy. The usual practice is to neutralize the charge with an electron flood gun and correct by setting the C 1s of adventitious hydrocarbon on the surface to a value such as 284.8 eV, but this reference value differs slightly between sources. Surfaces also become contaminated quickly, so hydrocarbons or oxygen picked up during sample handling and storage change the results. It is important to record how the measured surface was prepared.

faq.q: How deep does XPS see?
faq.a: Photoelectrons can escape without scattering from depths of roughly a few nm, so XPS gives information from the top few nm of the surface. Deeper regions are examined by depth profiling, measuring while sputtering with ions.

faq.q: Can XPS measure hydrogen?
faq.a: No. Hydrogen and helium have small photoionization cross sections and no core levels. The presence of hydrogen is inferred indirectly, for example from the chemical shifts of carbon and oxygen.

faq.q: How do you choose between XPS and EDS?
faq.a: XPS is suited to examining the elements and chemical states of the top few nm of a surface, averaged over a wide area; EDS is suited to examining the elements of tiny regions seen in the SEM, over a depth of about 1 µm depending on the accelerating voltage and sample.

エネルギー分散型X線分光.desc: A method (EDS) that analyzes elements by measuring, by energy, the characteristic X-rays generated by an electron beam. Attached to an SEM it analyzes tiny regions; the analysis depth depends on conditions but is about 1 µm.

ヒュッケル則.desc: The rule that a cyclic, planar, fully conjugated molecule is especially stable, that is, aromatic, when it has 4n + 2 π electrons (2, 6, 10 …). Benzene, pyridine and furan have six π electrons.

about.p: According to Hückel's rule, four conditions are needed for a molecule to be especially stabilized as aromatic: it must be cyclic, it must be planar, every ring atom must have a p orbital in unbroken conjugation, and the number of π electrons must be 4n + 2 (n = 0, 1, 2 …). Benzene, with six π electrons (n = 1), is the classic example. A planar conjugated ring with 4n π electrons is instead destabilized and is called antiaromatic. Cyclooctatetraene has eight π electrons, but it avoids antiaromaticity by not being planar and adopting a tub shape.

In heterocycles, what matters is whether a heteroatom's lone pair counts as π electrons. The nitrogen of pyridine contributes one electron to a p orbital as part of a double bond, and its lone pair, in an sp² orbital in the plane of the ring, is not counted. The nitrogen of pyrrole forms three σ bonds (to two carbons and a hydrogen) and puts its lone pair in a p orbital, contributing two electrons, for 4 + 2 = 6 π electrons. The oxygen of furan has two lone pairs; only the one in a p orbital is counted, and the other stays in the plane.

Hückel's rule applies to ions as well as neutral molecules. 1,3-Cyclopentadiene is not aromatic because of its sp³ CH2, but the cyclopentadienide ion C5H5⁻, formed by losing H⁺, has p orbitals on all five carbons and is aromatic with six π electrons. This is why cyclopentadiene has a pKa of about 16, very acidic for a hydrocarbon. Likewise, the cycloheptatrienyl cation (tropylium ion) C7H7⁺ is a 6π-electron aromatic species and is stable for a cation.

faq.q: Can a molecule be aromatic without exactly six π electrons?
faq.a: Yes. With n = 0 in 4n + 2 there are two, and with n = 2 there are ten. The cyclopropenyl cation C3H3⁺ is aromatic with two π electrons, and naphthalene with ten.

faq.q: Why does the lone pair on pyrrole's nitrogen join the π system?
faq.a: Once the nitrogen forms three σ bonds to two carbons and a hydrogen, putting the remaining pair in a p orbital makes the whole ring a 6π-electron aromatic system, which is a large stabilization. In exchange, nearly all of its basicity is lost.

faq.q: How can you check whether a compound is aromatic?
faq.a: Useful signs are that ring protons appear downfield in ¹H NMR (around δ 6.5–8.5) because of the ring current, that the compound tends to undergo substitution rather than addition, and that its heat of hydrogenation is smaller than expected.

複素環式化合物.desc: A cyclic compound with atoms other than carbon (nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur and so on) in the ring. Examples include pyridine, pyrrole, furan and imidazole, and the purines and pyrimidines of the nucleobases.

等電点.desc: The pH (pI) at which the net charge of an amino acid or protein is zero. For an amino acid it is the average of the two pKa values on either side of the net-zero form; for glycine it is about 6.0.

about.p: An amino acid is a fully protonated cation in acidic solution and a deprotonated anion in basic solution, and in between the zwitterion, with zero net charge, predominates. The isoelectric point pI is the average of the pKa values of the two dissociation steps on either side of this net-zero form. For glycine (pKa 2.34 and 9.60), pI = (2.34 + 9.60)/2 = 5.97. For amino acids with acidic or basic side chains, decide which two pKa values bracket the net-zero form by following the changes in charge step by step.

For amino acids with a carboxy group in the side chain, such as aspartic acid and glutamic acid, the pI is the average of the pKa values of the α-carboxy and side-chain carboxy groups, which is low, about 2.8 for aspartic acid. For amino acids with basic side chains, such as lysine and arginine, the pI is the average of the pKa values of the two ammonium (or similar) groups, which is high, about 9.7 for lysine. Averaging all three pKa values is a common mistake; it is important to check which form has zero net charge.

When the solution pH is below the pI, amino acids and proteins are positively charged, and when it is above, negatively charged. In electrophoresis, positively charged species move toward the cathode and negatively charged ones toward the anode, and at a pH equal to the pI they hardly move. In a gel with a pH gradient, each protein stops and collects at the position of its own pI, which allows high-resolution separation as isoelectric focusing. Also, at the isoelectric point the electrostatic repulsion between protein molecules is small and solubility tends to fall, which is used in isoelectric precipitation.

faq.q: Does an amino acid carry no charge at its isoelectric point?
faq.a: Almost all of it is the zwitterion, with one positive and one negative charge in the same molecule, so the net charge is zero. The charges themselves do not disappear.

faq.q: Is the pI just the average of all three pKa values?
faq.a: No. Average only the pKa values of the two steps on either side of the form with zero net charge. For aspartic acid that is the average of 1.88 and 3.65, about 2.77.

faq.q: What determines the isoelectric point of a protein?
faq.a: It is set by the numbers of acidic and basic side chains on the surface and their individual pKa values, and a rough value can be estimated by calculation. Actual values are measured by isoelectric focusing and similar methods.

双性イオン.desc: An ion that carries one positive and one negative charge within the same molecule and is electrically neutral overall. Amino acids take the form H3N⁺−CHR−COO⁻ in water and in the solid.

ペプチド結合.desc: The amide bond −CO−NH− formed when water is lost from the carboxy group of one amino acid and the amino group of another. Resonance gives the C−N bond partial double-bond character and holds it planar.

アノマー.desc: Either of two isomers that differ only in the configuration at the anomeric carbon (C1 of glucose), which becomes a new stereocenter when a sugar cyclizes. The α and β forms interconvert in water and show mutarotation.

相補的塩基対.desc: A fixed pair formed by nucleic acid bases through hydrogen bonding. In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds and guanine with cytosine through three; in RNA, uracil replaces thymine.

けん化価.desc: The mass (mg) of potassium hydroxide needed to saponify 1 g of a fat or oil. It is larger the smaller the average molecular weight of the constituent fatty acids; for tripalmitin it is about 209.

固相抽出.desc: Sample preparation in which a sample solution is passed through a stationary phase packed in a cartridge to retain the analytes, which are then washed and eluted with a small volume of solvent (SPE). It removes interferences and concentrates at the same time.

分配比.desc: In liquid–liquid extraction, the ratio of the total concentrations of a substance in the two phases (organic/aqueous). It includes all neutral and ionized forms, so for acids and bases it changes with the pH of the aqueous phase.

マイクロ波分解.desc: A method of digesting a sample with acid in a closed vessel heated by microwaves. Under pressure the acid can be heated above its boiling point, and losses of volatile elements and contamination are small.

標準添加法.desc: A method that measures the sample itself with known amounts of analyte added stepwise and finds the concentration by extending the line of signal versus amount added to zero signal. It corrects for changes in sensitivity caused by the matrix.

about.p: In the standard addition method, the sample solution is divided into several equal portions, standard is added to them in steps such as 0, 1, 2 and 3, and each is measured. Plotting signal on the vertical axis against amount added on the horizontal axis gives a line raised by the signal from the analyte already in the sample. The magnitude of the horizontal-axis intercept, where this line is extended to zero signal, is the concentration in the sample solution. With a single addition, Cx = ΔC × S0/(S1 − S0), but linearity cannot then be checked, so multiple additions are the norm.

about.h: Errors it can and cannot correct
about.p: Because the standards are measured in the same matrix as the sample, the standard addition method corrects proportional effects, in which coexisting salts and acids, viscosity, suppression of ionization in the plasma and so on change the sensitivity (slope). Additive effects such as spectral overlap and background, which add a constant signal regardless of concentration, are not corrected and remain as a positive error. These must be removed separately by background correction, subtraction of a blank, or choice of a different measurement wavelength or isotope.

about.h: Points to watch when using it
about.p: Because the concentration is found by extrapolation, the method assumes that the signal is proportional to concentration over the range of the additions. The amounts added are about one to several times the amount in the sample and should not exceed the linear range of the calibration. If the additions change the volume, correct for the dilution or prepare the solutions to the same final volume. Several solutions are made for each sample, which takes effort, so routine analyses with many samples often use matrix-matched external standards or the internal standard method instead.

faq.q: How does it differ from the internal standard method?
