faq.a: The internal standard method adds a different substance and takes the ratio of signals to cancel variations in injection volume and sensitivity. The standard addition method adds the analyte itself to the sample and directly finds the sensitivity in that sample.

faq.q: Is a single addition enough?
faq.a: The calculation can be done, but linearity and the effect of the blank cannot be checked. The basic approach is to draw a line through at least two or three levels of addition.

faq.q: What if the sample has a blank that gives a signal of its own?
faq.a: A blank from reagents and the like is an additive effect, so standard addition does not correct for it. Subtract the blank signal before calculating.

室内再現精度.desc: The precision when measurements are repeated within the same laboratory while changing the day, analyst, instrument and so on. Its scatter is usually larger than that of repeatability, measured under the same conditions within a short time.

回収率.desc: The fraction of a known added amount that is recovered when a spiked sample is analyzed. It is found as (result for spiked sample − result for unspiked sample)/amount added × 100 and reflects trueness including sample preparation.

測定の不確かさ.desc: A quantity expressing the spread of values around a measurement result within which the true value may lie. The standard uncertainties of the factors are combined, and results are often reported with the expanded uncertainty using a coverage factor k = 2.

about.p: Measurement uncertainty expresses, in the form of a standard deviation, how wide a range should be allowed around a measurement result. An error is the difference from the true value, which in practice cannot be found because the true value is unknown; uncertainty, by contrast, can be evaluated from the information at hand. It is evaluated in two ways: Type A, statistically from the scatter of repeated measurements, and Type B, from values in calibration certificates, tolerances of glassware, the stated purity of reference materials and so on. Both are expressed as standard uncertainties before they are combined.

When a result y is calculated from several quantities, the standard uncertainty of each factor is weighted by its sensitivity coefficient and they are combined as the square root of the sum of squares. For products and quotients of mutually uncorrelated quantities, the relative combined standard uncertainty is the square root of the sum of the squares of the relative standard uncertainties. For example, with four factors of 0.20%, 0.10%, 0.15% and 0.50%, it is √0.3225 = 0.57%. Because the terms are squared before adding, the largest factor tends to dominate, and improving small factors has little effect.

The combined standard uncertainty uc multiplied by a coverage factor k is called the expanded uncertainty, U = k·uc; assuming a normal distribution, k = 2 gives a level of confidence of about 95%. Results are reported together with the value of k, as in "12.3 ± 0.2 mg/L (k = 2)". In estimating uncertainty it is important to list every factor that affects the result, such as losses in sample preparation, the calibration curve, preparation of standards and repeatability; drawing up this list is the heart of the evaluation.

faq.q: Are error and uncertainty the same thing?
faq.a: No. Error is the difference between a measured value and the true value, which cannot be found because the true value is unknown. Uncertainty is the width of scatter that should be allowed for in the result, and it can be evaluated from the information available.

faq.q: Why use the square root of the sum of squares instead of simply adding?
faq.a: Because scatter from mutually independent factors can partly cancel by chance, it is the variances (squares of the standard deviations) that add. Simply adding overestimates the uncertainty.

faq.q: Must k = 2 always be used?
faq.a: It is widely used by convention, but when the degrees of freedom are small a larger k may be chosen from the t distribution. The value of k used is stated in the report.

グラブス検定.desc: A test that judges whether the largest or smallest value in a data set is an outlier by comparing G = |x − x̄|/s with a critical value. The mean and standard deviation are found from all the data, including the suspect value.

18電子則.desc: The rule of thumb that transition-metal complexes tend to be stable when the metal's d electrons plus the electrons donated by the ligands total 18. Square-planar d⁸ complexes and some others have 16 electrons.

about.p: The orbitals that hold a transition metal's valence electrons are the 5 (n−1)d orbitals, 1 ns orbital and 3 np orbitals, 9 in all. When all of them are filled with electron pairs, the count is 18, and the 18-electron rule regards this as a stable configuration, like that of a noble gas. Carbonyl complexes such as Cr(CO)6, Fe(CO)5 and Ni(CO)4, and ferrocene, have 18 electrons and are stable compounds that can be isolated and stored; ferrocene in particular is stable even in air. It is easiest to think of it as the octet rule (8 electrons) used for main-group elements in organic compounds, extended to include the d orbitals.

In the commonly used ionic model, you first treat the ligands as closed-shell species such as CH3⁻, Cl⁻, H⁻ and C5H5⁻ and determine the metal's oxidation state. The metal's d-electron count is the group number minus the oxidation state; for example, Rh(I) is 9 − 1 = 8, d⁸. Adding the electrons donated by each ligand (2 for CO, PR3, Cl⁻ and CH3⁻, and 6 for η⁵-C5H5⁻) gives the valence electron count. The covalent model, which treats the ligands as neutral, gives the same count when done correctly.

The 18-electron rule is only a rule of thumb, and there are many exceptions. d⁸ metals such as Rh(I), Ir(I), Pd(II) and Pt(II) readily form square-planar 16-electron complexes; Wilkinson's catalyst, RhCl(PPh3)3, and Vaska's complex are examples. In catalytic reactions, a coordinatively unsaturated 16- or 14-electron complex often takes up the substrate at a vacant site, reaches 18 electrons by oxidative addition and returns by reductive elimination, so the reaction proceeds while the electron count shuttles between 16 and 18.

The 18-electron rule works best for low-oxidation-state organometallic complexes with strongly π-accepting ligands such as CO and phosphines. On the other hand, classical complexes with water or ammonia coordinated, such as [Cu(H2O)6]²⁺, and complexes of metals on the left of the periodic table (such as Ti and Zr) include many stable compounds that do not have 18 electrons. When bulky ligands crowd the metal, complexes are also stable with fewer electrons. The electron count is best used as a starting point for predicting a complex's reactivity.

faq.q: How do I find the d-electron count?
faq.a: Subtract the oxidation state from the metal's group number. For example, Fe(II) of group 8 iron is d⁶, and Pd(0) of group 10 palladium is d¹⁰. There is no need to count the 4s electrons of the electron configuration separately.

faq.q: Are complexes without 18 electrons unstable?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Square-planar d⁸ complexes are stable with 16 electrons, and many classical complexes are stable without 18 electrons. The 18-electron rule is a guide for low-oxidation-state organometallic complexes.

faq.q: Why count electrons in catalytic reactions?
faq.a: Because it shows at which steps ligand dissociation or substrate coordination can occur. An 18-electron complex has no room for a substrate to approach, so it is thought to react only after a ligand leaves and it drops to 16 electrons or fewer.

酸化的付加.desc: An elementary step in which a metal inserts into an A−B bond to give M(A)(B). The metal's oxidation state and coordination number each rise by 2, and its d-electron count falls by 2. The first step of cross-coupling.

about.p: Oxidative addition is an elementary step in which a coordinatively unsaturated, low-oxidation-state metal complex M inserts into a bond A−B, such as H−H, C−X (X is a halogen) or C−H, giving M(A)(B). A and B are each counted as anionic ligands, so the metal's oxidation state rises by 2, its coordination number rises by 2 and its d-electron count falls by 2. The valence electron count rises by 2, so a 16-electron complex becomes 18 electrons and a 14-electron complex becomes 16. For example, Pd(0) reacts with Ar−Br to give Ar−Pd(II)−Br.

about.h: What controls how readily it occurs
about.p: Oxidative addition is a reaction in which electrons flow from the metal into the antibonding orbital of A−B, so it occurs more readily with electron-rich metals, and strongly electron-donating phosphine ligands speed it up. For aryl halides, the weaker the C−X bond, the more readily it occurs, in the order C−I > C−Br > C−Cl. Unreactive substrates such as aryl chlorides are handled with bulky, electron-rich ligands such as P(t-Bu)3, which form highly reactive complexes bearing only one ligand.

Nonpolar bonds such as H2 approach the metal side-on and add in a concerted way, and the 2 H atoms end up cis to each other. Highly polar alkyl halides such as CH3I often react by an SN2-type mechanism in which the metal attacks carbon as a nucleophile; the configuration at carbon is inverted, and the 2 ligands may end up trans. Addition of palladium to aryl halides is in many cases thought to involve concerted addition of a complex that has lost some of its ligands to the C−X bond of the arene.

faq.q: Why is it called "oxidative"?
faq.a: Because when the 2 added ligands are counted as anions, the metal's oxidation state rises by 2; that is, the metal is formally oxidized. In the reverse reaction the oxidation state falls by 2, so it is called reductive elimination.

faq.q: Which metals undergo oxidative addition readily?
faq.a: Electron-rich, low-oxidation-state metals that are also stable in the oxidation state 2 higher, such as Pd(0), Ni(0), Rh(I) and Ir(I). An 18-electron complex must first lose a ligand to become coordinatively unsaturated.

faq.q: Which step is rate-determining in cross-coupling?
faq.a: It depends on the substrate and ligand, but with unreactive substrates such as aryl chlorides, oxidative addition is often rate-determining. With bulky ligands, reductive elimination or transmetalation can be rate-determining.

還元的脱離.desc: An elementary step in which 2 ligands on a metal form a bond and leave; the reverse of oxidative addition. The oxidation state and coordination number each fall by 2, and it occurs between ligands cis to each other.

β-水素脱離.desc: An elementary step in which a hydrogen on the β carbon of a metal alkyl complex moves to the metal, giving a metal hydride and an alkene. It requires a vacant coordination site and a syn-coplanar arrangement.

移動挿入.desc: An elementary step in which an alkyl or similar group on a metal moves to an adjacent CO or alkene ligand to form a new bond. With CO a metal acyl complex forms and a vacant coordination site opens up.

π逆供与.desc: Bonding in which electrons flow from filled metal d orbitals into empty π* orbitals of ligands such as CO and alkenes. The ligand's multiple bond is weakened and the CO stretching wavenumber falls.

円錐角.desc: The apex angle of a cone, with the metal at its apex, that encloses a phosphine ligand; a measure of ligand bulk proposed by Tolman. About 145° for PPh3 and about 182° for P(t-Bu)3.

触媒回転頻度.desc: The number of times product is formed per catalyst molecule per unit time. It is found by dividing the turnover number TON by the reaction time and expressed in h⁻¹ or s⁻¹. Abbreviated TOF.

速度式.desc: An equation expressing how a reaction rate depends on the concentration of each substance. The orders a and b in v = k[A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ are determined by experiment, not from the coefficients of the chemical equation.

律速段階.desc: In a multistep reaction, the slowest step, which sets the overall rate. The structure of its transition state shows up in the rate law, isotope effects and substituent effects.

擬一次反応.desc: A method of treating a second-order reaction as first order by adding one reactant in large excess so that its concentration stays nearly constant. The apparent rate constant is k' = k[excess substance].

アレニウスの式.desc: The equation k = A exp(−Ea/RT) expressing the temperature dependence of a rate constant. The activation energy Ea is obtained from the slope of the straight line in a plot of ln k against 1/T.

速度論的同位体効果.desc: The ratio of rate constants when an atom is replaced by its isotope. When a C−H bond breaks in the rate-determining step, kH/kD is about 2–7 at room temperature, which is used to infer reaction mechanisms.

about.p: Replacing hydrogen with deuterium hardly changes the electronic state or the potential energy surface. What changes is the vibrational frequency: the heavier C−D bond vibrates at a lower frequency than the C−H bond and has a lower zero-point vibrational energy. Stretching wavenumbers are about 3000 cm⁻¹ for C−H and about 2200 cm⁻¹ for C−D. If this bond breaks in the transition state and its stretching vibration disappears, the molecule with C−D has a larger activation energy, by the amount its zero-point energy is lower, and reacts more slowly.

The effect when the bond containing the isotope itself breaks or forms in the rate-determining step is called a primary isotope effect. For C−H versus C−D, the upper limit at room temperature estimated from the zero-point energy difference is about kH/kD ≈ 7, and values of 2–7 are commonly observed in practice. In E2 reactions, for example, the β C−H breaks in the rate-determining step, giving large values, whereas in aromatic nitration the C−H breaks after the rate-determining step, so kH/kD is almost 1. In reactions with significant proton tunneling it can exceed 10.

The small effect of replacing a C−H near the reaction center, rather than the bond that breaks, with deuterium is called a secondary isotope effect, with kH/kD of about 0.8–1.2. It tends to be slightly greater than 1 in SN1 reactions, where the reacting carbon changes from sp³ to sp², and less than 1 (an inverse isotope effect) in additions, where it changes from sp² to sp³, giving a clue to the change in hybridization in the transition state. The solvent isotope effect, on changing the solvent from H2O to D2O, is used to find out whether proton transfer is involved in the rate-determining step.

faq.q: If kH/kD is 1, does that mean the C−H bond is not broken?
faq.a: It means it is not broken in the rate-determining step. If the C−H bond breaks in a fast step after the rate-determining step, kH/kD is almost 1 even though the C−H breaks in the overall reaction.

faq.q: How is it measured?
faq.a: Either the rate constants of the deuterated and ordinary substrates are measured separately, or the two are mixed and allowed to react competitively, and the isotope ratio of the products is examined by mass spectrometry or NMR. Competition experiments reduce errors from differences in conditions.

faq.q: Do isotopes other than deuterium have effects?
faq.a: Yes. They occur with ¹²C versus ¹³C, for example, but the mass ratio is small, so the effect is also small, a few percent. The effect for H versus D, where the mass doubles, is the largest and most widely used.

ハメット則.desc: The relationship log(kX/kH) = ρσ for rate constants or equilibrium constants of benzene derivatives with meta or para substituents. The sign and size of ρ reveal the charge in the transition state.

about.p: Hammett quantified the electronic effects of substituents using the acid dissociation constants of substituted benzoic acids in water at 25 °C as the reference. σ = log(KX/KH), where KH is the acid dissociation constant of benzoic acid and KX that of the substituted benzoic acid. Electron-withdrawing groups stabilize the conjugate base, the carboxylate, and strengthen the acid, so σ is positive; for electron-donating groups it is negative. Typical σp values are 0.78 for nitro, 0.23 for chlorine, −0.17 for methyl and −0.27 for methoxy. Even for the same substituent, resonance acts differently at the meta and para positions, so σm and σp differ.

When the logarithms of the rate constants or equilibrium constants of other reactions are plotted against σ, the result is often a straight line, and its slope is the reaction constant ρ. A positive ρ means electron-withdrawing groups speed up the reaction and that negative charge forms or increases at the reaction center in the transition state. A negative ρ means a reaction in which positive charge develops. The larger |ρ|, the larger the change in charge, or the closer to the aromatic ring the charge develops. The ρ for alkaline hydrolysis of ethyl benzoates is about +2.5, reflecting the negative charge of the tetrahedral intermediate.

about.h: σ⁺ and σ⁻, and deviations from linearity
about.p: In reactions where positive charge can resonate directly with a para substituent, such as those forming benzylic carbocations, ordinary σ does not give a good straight line, and σ⁺, determined from the solvolysis of cumyl chlorides, is used instead. Conversely, when negative charge resonates directly, as with phenoxides, σ⁻ is used. When a plot bends partway, the rate-determining step or the mechanism may be changing with the substituent. Ortho substituents add steric effects, so they are normally not treated with the Hammett equation.

faq.q: What does the sign of ρ tell me?
faq.a: It tells you the sign of the charge that develops at the reaction center in the transition state of the rate-determining step. If ρ is positive, negative charge develops and electron-withdrawing groups speed the reaction; if ρ is negative, positive charge develops and electron-donating groups speed it.

faq.q: What does a ρ greater than 1 mean?
faq.a: It means the reaction is more strongly affected by substituents than the reference ionization of benzoic acid. With ρ = 2.5, for example, a difference of 0.4 in σ changes the rate constant 10-fold.

faq.q: Why can't it be used for ortho-substituted compounds?
faq.a: Ortho substituents are close to the reaction center, and steric effects, hydrogen bonding and the like overlap with the electronic effect, so σ alone cannot describe them.

定常状態近似.desc: The approximation that the concentration of a reactive intermediate is small and nearly constant, so its rates of formation and consumption are set equal. Used to derive the rate laws of multistep reactions.

カーティン・ハメットの原理.desc: The principle that when rapidly interconverting isomers each give a different product, the product ratio is set not by the population ratio of the isomers but by the free-energy difference between the transition states.

フロンティア軌道.desc: A molecule's HOMO (highest occupied molecular orbital) and LUMO (lowest unoccupied molecular orbital). Reactivity and regioselectivity are explained by the interaction of one molecule's HOMO with the other's LUMO.

about.p: Of a molecule's orbitals, the highest-energy filled one is called the HOMO (highest occupied molecular orbital) and the lowest empty one the LUMO (lowest unoccupied molecular orbital); together they are called the frontier orbitals. Kenichi Fukui showed that how readily a reaction occurs, and where, is determined mainly by the properties of these two orbitals. A nucleophile donates electrons from its HOMO, and an electrophile accepts them into its LUMO. The higher the HOMO, the more readily electrons are donated, and the lower the LUMO, the more readily they are accepted.

about.h: What sets the size of the interaction
about.p: When one molecule's HOMO overlaps with the other's LUMO, two electrons enter the newly formed bonding orbital and the system is stabilized. This stabilization is greater the smaller the energy gap between the two orbitals, and the larger the orbital coefficients (sizes) on the reacting atoms and the better their phases match. Overlap between two filled HOMOs is a four-electron repulsion and forms no bond. Considering how substituents change orbital energies and coefficients lets you predict the rate and direction of reactions.

In an ordinary Diels–Alder reaction, the pair of diene HOMO and dienophile LUMO mainly operates (normal electron demand). An electron-withdrawing group on the dienophile lowers its LUMO and an electron-donating group on the diene raises its HOMO, and both make the reaction faster. Regioselectivity is explained by bonding between the termini with the largest coefficients: 1-substituted dienes mainly give the "ortho" product and 2-substituted dienes the "para" product. The endo rule is also explained by a secondary overlap between the orbitals of the carbonyl group and the diene.

faq.q: Why is it enough to consider only the HOMO and LUMO?
faq.a: When all orbital interactions are added up, the HOMO–LUMO pair, with its small energy gap, contributes the most. It is not an exact calculation, but it is often a good enough approximation for grasping trends in reactivity and selectivity.

faq.q: What happens when a HOMO overlaps with a HOMO?
faq.a: Both contain two electrons, so both the resulting bonding and antibonding orbitals are filled, and overall there is no stabilization but rather repulsion. It therefore does not work toward bond formation.

faq.q: Can frontier orbitals be used for reactions other than pericyclic ones?
faq.a: Yes. Thinking of a nucleophile's HOMO attacking a LUMO such as the π* of a carbonyl group or the σ* of a C−X bond explains the backside attack of the SN2 reaction and the site of nucleophilic addition.

ヒュッケル分子軌道法.desc: A simple molecular orbital method that treats only π electrons and represents the interaction between adjacent carbons by the resonance integral β. It gives π orbital energies in the form α + xβ.

非局在化エネルギー.desc: The size of the stabilization from π electrons spreading over the whole molecule. It is found by comparison with a set of isolated double bonds; in Hückel theory it is 0.472|β| for butadiene and 2|β| for benzene.

反芳香族性.desc: The property by which a cyclic, planar, conjugated system with 4n π electrons fails to form a closed shell and is destabilized. Cyclobutadiene is the typical example, and a paratropic ring current appears in ¹H NMR.

エンド則.desc: The empirical rule that in the Diels–Alder reaction the endo adduct, formed through a transition state in which the dienophile's unsaturated substituent points toward the diene's π system, is kinetically favored. It is explained by secondary orbital interactions.

ウッドワード-ホフマン則.desc: Rules that determine from orbital symmetry whether a concerted pericyclic reaction is thermally or photochemically allowed or forbidden. Thermal electrocyclic reactions are conrotatory with 4n electrons and disrotatory with 4n + 2.

about.p: Woodward and Hoffmann showed that in a concerted pericyclic reaction, the phases (symmetry) of the orbitals must connect continuously from reactants to products. If the orbitals overlap in phase at both ends where bonds form, the reaction is allowed and proceeds with a low activation energy. If the phases do not match it is forbidden and proceeds poorly in a concerted way. The frontier-orbital method based on the shape of the HOMO, orbital correlation diagrams, and the method based on the aromaticity of the transition state all give the same conclusions.

A reaction in which the two ends of a conjugated polyene bond to form a ring (and the reverse ring opening) is called an electrocyclic reaction. Thermally, if the number of π electrons involved is 4n (butadiene and cyclobutene), the ends rotate in the same direction, conrotatory; if it is 4n + 2 (hexatriene and cyclohexadiene), they rotate in opposite directions, disrotatory. Photoexcitation changes the HOMO to the next orbital up, so the mode of rotation swaps. The configuration of the substituents determines whether the product is cis or trans, and the reaction is stereospecific.

By the generalized rule, a reaction is thermally allowed if the total number of suprafacial (4q + 2)-electron components and antarafacial 4r-electron components is odd. The Diels–Alder reaction [π4s + π2s] has one and is allowed, while [π2s + π2s] for two ethylenes has two and is thermally forbidden, proceeding photochemically. The same reasoning is used for sigmatropic rearrangements, in which a σ bond migrates: [3,3] rearrangements such as the Cope and Claisen rearrangements and suprafacial [1,5]-hydrogen shifts are thermally allowed.

faq.q: Do "forbidden" reactions never occur at all?
faq.a: It means the energy barrier of the concerted pathway is high; they can occur through stepwise pathways via radicals and the like, or at higher temperatures. Many thermally forbidden reactions are photochemically allowed.

faq.q: How do you tell conrotatory from disrotatory?
faq.a: If the bonds at the two ends that open or close the ring rotate in the same direction (both clockwise, for example), the motion is conrotatory; if they rotate in opposite directions, it is disrotatory. Thermally, it is conrotatory with 4n π electrons and disrotatory with 4n + 2.

faq.q: How are the Woodward–Hoffmann rules related to frontier orbitals?
faq.a: Kenichi Fukui's frontier orbital theory gives the same selection rules by looking at the phases at the two ends of the HOMO. Hoffmann and Fukui received the 1981 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work.

電子環状反応.desc: A concerted reaction in which the two ends of a conjugated polyene join through a σ bond to form a ring, and the reverse ring opening. Conrotatory and disrotatory modes swap between heat and light, and the reaction is stereospecific.

シグマトロピー転位.desc: A concerted rearrangement in which a σ bond adjacent to a π system migrates across the π system and forms anew at another position. Examples are the [3,3] Cope and Claisen rearrangements and [1,5]-hydrogen shifts.

構造活性相関.desc: The relationship between a compound's chemical structure and its biological activity (SAR). By changing the structure step by step and comparing activities, the parts needed for activity are distinguished from those that can be improved.

about.p: The structure–activity relationship (SAR) is the relationship between a compound's chemical structure and its biological activity, a way of thinking that underlies drug design. Once an active lead compound is found, analogs are synthesized in which the type or position of substituents, ring size, configuration and so on are changed one at a time, and their activities are measured. From the results, the parts essential for activity (the pharmacophore), the parts that can be changed while keeping activity, and the parts whose change raises activity are distinguished, and the compound is optimized toward greater potency and selectivity.

In SAR it is important to compare the potencies of compounds with condition-independent quantities. The IC50 for enzyme inhibition depends on measurement conditions such as substrate concentration, so for competitive inhibition it is converted to Ki with the Cheng–Prusoff equation and compared as pKi (−log Ki). An increase of 1 in pKi means binding is 10 times stronger. Because making a molecule larger tends to raise potency, ligand efficiency, the binding energy per heavy atom, is also examined to judge whether an improvement is worth the added size.

Expressing activity as an equation in physical-property values is called a quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR). In Hansch analysis, log(1/C) is expressed as a linear combination of the hydrophobic substituent constant π, the Hammett constant σ for electronic effects, steric constants and so on, to find which properties govern activity. Today calculations based on the three-dimensional structures of molecules and target proteins are also widely used, but all of them start from experimental SAR data. These equations rest on the premise that substituent effects are roughly additive.

faq.q: What is the difference between SAR and QSAR?
faq.a: SAR captures the relationship between changes in structure and changes in activity qualitatively, while QSAR expresses it quantitatively as an equation using numerical values such as π and σ.

faq.q: Can activity change suddenly and greatly?
faq.a: Yes. A pair in which a slight structural difference changes activity greatly is called an activity cliff, and it is a clue to finding interactions important for binding. Cases in which a single methyl group raises activity greatly are also known.

faq.q: Is activity the only thing examined in SAR?
faq.a: No. The relationships of solubility, membrane permeability, metabolic stability, toxicity and so on with structure are also examined, and compounds are optimized while balancing these against activity. These are sometimes collectively called structure–property relationships.

ファーマコフォア.desc: The features needed to bind the target and show activity, such as hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, hydrophobic regions and charges, together with their three-dimensional arrangement. Compounds with different skeletons can share one.

リピンスキーの5の法則.desc: The empirical rule that exceeding two or more of molecular weight 500, logP 5, 5 hydrogen-bond donors and 10 acceptors makes poor oral absorption or membrane permeation likely.

about.h: What the rule of five says
about.p: Lipinski's rule of five is an empirical rule compiled in 1997 by examining the properties of drugs that had been used orally. If two or more of four criteria apply, molecular weight over 500, logP over 5, more than 5 hydrogen-bond donors (the number of OH and NH) and more than 10 hydrogen-bond acceptors (the number of N and O), absorption or membrane permeation is taken to be likely to be poor. It gets its name because the threshold numbers are all multiples of five. It later came to be used to screen many drug candidates.

An oral drug must dissolve in the water of the gastrointestinal tract and then pass through lipid cell membranes into the blood. If a molecule is too large or has too many hydrogen-bonding groups, a lot of energy is needed to break its hydrogen bonds with water as it enters the membrane, so it permeates poorly. On the other hand, if logP is too large, it dissolves poorly in water. The rule of five expresses, in easily counted numbers, a guide for balancing dissolving with passing through membranes. Empirically, too, membrane permeability tends to fall as the molecular weight and the number of hydrogen bonds increase.

about.h: How to use it and its limits
about.p: The rule of five is a simple guide for screening candidate compounds: following it does not guarantee absorption, and violating it does not mean a compound cannot become an oral drug. There are many exceptions among drugs carried by transporters and large molecules derived from natural products. It is used together with Veber's criteria, which add the number of rotatable bonds (10 or fewer) and polar surface area (140 Å² or less), and the "rule of three", a guide for choosing fragments. What matters is to think about the balance of solubility and permeability behind the thresholds.

faq.q: How is a compound judged if only one criterion is exceeded?
faq.a: With only one, the rule of five does not immediately flag a problem. Exceeding two or more makes poor absorption likely, so revising the structure or formulation measures are considered.

faq.q: How are hydrogen-bond acceptors counted?
faq.a: In Lipinski's original definition, the number of acceptors is the total number of nitrogen and oxygen atoms. Donors are the number of OH and NH; NH2 is counted as two in some conventions and as one in others.

faq.q: Is the rule of five used for injectable drugs too?
faq.a: The rule of five is a guide for estimating oral absorption, so it is not applied as such to drugs given by injection or applied locally.

オクタノール/水分配係数.desc: The ratio P of the concentrations of the neutral compound when it partitions between 1-octanol and water. Its common logarithm, logP, expresses lipophilicity and is used as a guide to membrane permeation, absorption and metabolism.

分布係数.desc: The ratio D of the concentrations of the whole compound, including the ionized form, in the octanol and aqueous phases. Its common logarithm, logD, depends on pH; for a weak acid it becomes smaller as the pH rises.

プロドラッグ.desc: A compound designed to have little activity itself and to be converted into the active form in the body by enzymes or chemical reactions. It is used to improve absorption, water solubility or delivery to the site of action.

生物学的等価体.desc: An atom or group similar in size, shape, charge distribution and so on, so that biological activity is kept after replacement. Examples are tetrazole for a carboxy group and fluorine for hydrogen.

ユートマー.desc: Of the enantiomers of a chiral drug, the one with higher desired activity. The less active one is called the distomer, and the ratio of their activities the eudismic ratio.

グリーンケミストリー.desc: The idea of designing chemical products and processes so that hazardous substances and waste are not generated in the first place, rather than treated afterwards. It is summarized in the 12 principles of Anastas and Warner.

about.p: Green chemistry is the idea of designing chemical products and their manufacturing processes so that as little hazardous material and waste as possible is generated. In 1998 Anastas and Warner summarized it in 12 principles, including waste prevention, syntheses with high atom economy, use of less hazardous substances and solvents, energy efficiency, renewable feedstocks, catalysts in preference to stoichiometric reagents, design of products that degrade readily, and accident prevention. All the principles share the idea of not causing problems in the first place rather than dealing with them later.

Comparing processes against the principles needs numerical metrics. Atom economy, calculated from the reaction equation, shows the fraction of atoms that end up in the desired product but does not include the yield or solvents. The E-factor, the mass of waste per kg of product, and the process mass intensity (PMI), the mass of all materials put in divided by the mass of product, are therefore used. In pharmaceutical processes solvents and water often make up most of the input, so reducing and recovering solvents is the most effective improvement.

The 12 principles also include choosing less hazardous substances and conditions to prevent accidents such as explosions, fires and releases of harmful materials. In process chemistry, the heat of reaction is measured to estimate the temperature rise if cooling fails, and if necessary heat release is controlled by adding a reagent gradually, or continuous flow synthesis, which keeps little hazardous material in the reactor, is chosen. Reducing solvent, for example, lowers both the waste and the risk of fire. Reducing waste and preventing accidents are not separate efforts; it is important to consider both at the same design stage.

faq.q: How does green chemistry differ from environmental chemistry?
faq.a: Environmental chemistry studies the distribution, reactions and effects of substances in the environment. Green chemistry is the idea of designing products and processes that do not generate hazardous substances or waste in the first place, and it is something chemists work on at the synthesis and manufacturing stage.

faq.q: Is a reaction green if its atom economy is high?
faq.a: Atom economy is found from the reaction equation alone and does not include the yield, solvents, excess reagents or waste from purification. It needs to be assessed together with the E-factor, PMI, safety and energy use.

faq.q: Why does using a catalyst reduce waste?
faq.a: A stoichiometric reagent produces the same amount of by-product every time the reaction runs, whereas a catalyst is regenerated and works repeatedly, so only a small amount is needed. Raising selectivity and suppressing side reactions is another advantage.

E-ファクター.desc: The mass of waste (kg) generated per kg of product. A metric proposed by Sheldon; the smaller the value, the less waste. It is often calculated excluding water.

about.p: The E-factor is a metric proposed by Sheldon in 1992, expressed as E = mass of waste ÷ mass of product. Waste includes raw materials and reagents that did not become product, by-products, solvent not recovered and materials used in workup; solvent recovered and reused is not counted. The original definition excludes water, because including it makes the values so large that they are hard to compare, but values including water are sometimes reported alongside, so it is necessary to check which basis is used before comparing. The ideal value is 0.

Sheldon gave typical values by industry sector: below 0.1 for oil refining, from below 1 to about 5 for bulk chemicals, 5 to over 50 for fine chemicals and 25 to over 100 for pharmaceuticals. Pharmaceuticals have complex structures that need multistep syntheses and must reach high purity, so the waste per unit of product is large. On the other hand, bulk chemicals are produced in quantities orders of magnitude larger, so the ranking changes when total waste is compared. The E-factor is strictly a ratio expressing efficiency per unit of product.

about.h: Relation to PMI and atom economy
about.p: The process mass intensity, PMI, is the mass of all materials put in divided by the mass of product; counted on the same basis, E = PMI − 1. Because PMI is counted from the input side, it is easy to find without having to decide what counts as waste, and it is widely used in the pharmaceutical industry. Atom economy is a theoretical value calculated from the reaction equation, while the E-factor is the result of an actual process. Even a reaction with 100% atom economy can have a large E-factor because of waste from solvents and purification.

faq.q: Is water counted as waste?
faq.a: Not in Sheldon's original definition. Wastewater treatment also carries a burden, however, so values including water are sometimes reported alongside. When comparing, use the same basis.

faq.q: Can the E-factor be smaller than 1?
faq.a: Yes. In processes such as oil refining, with almost no by-products or solvent losses, it can be below 0.1. The ideal value is 0, with no waste at all.

faq.q: Is the toxicity of the waste taken into account?
faq.a: The E-factor counts mass only, so differences in toxicity are not reflected. Because it counts 1 kg of a heavy-metal salt the same as 1 kg of common salt, metrics weighted by toxicity or environmental impact have also been proposed.

プロセス質量強度.desc: The total mass of reactants, reagents, solvents and water put into a process divided by the mass of product. Widely used in the pharmaceutical industry; it is related to the E-factor on the same basis by PMI = E + 1.

溶媒選択ガイド.desc: A list that assesses solvents by toxicity, flammability, environmental impact, ease of recovery and so on, and sorts them into classes such as recommended, problematic and to be avoided. Pharmaceutical companies and others produce them.

超臨界二酸化炭素.desc: Carbon dioxide above its critical point (about 31℃, about 7.4 MPa). Its dissolving power can be tuned by changing its density and it is removed by depressurization, so it is used as a solvent for extraction and reactions.

断熱温度上昇.desc: The temperature increase if all the heat of reaction goes into heating the reaction mixture. It is used to estimate MTSR, the maximum temperature that can be reached if cooling fails.

連続フロー合成.desc: A method of running reactions while starting materials flow continuously through narrow tubes or channels. Heat is easy to remove and little hazardous material is in the reactor, so hazardous reactions are easier to run safely.

超分子化学.desc: The chemistry of structures formed when molecules come together through noncovalent interactions such as hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions, and of their functions. Molecular recognition and self-assembly are its central themes.

水素結合.desc: An interaction in which a hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom is attracted to a lone pair on another atom. Between neutral molecules it is a few to a few tens of kJ/mol, and it is directional.

π-π相互作用.desc: The attraction between aromatic rings. It consists of dispersion forces and electrostatic interactions between quadrupoles, and the rings tend to adopt offset parallel-displaced or T-shaped arrangements.

クラウンエーテル.desc: A macrocyclic polyether with −CH2CH2O− as the repeating unit. The oxygens inside the ring selectively and strongly take up cations that fit the size of the cavity.

about.p: Crown ethers are macrocyclic polyethers with −CH2CH2O− as the repeating unit, discovered by Pedersen in 1967. They are named for their resemblance to a crown and are called by the total number of ring atoms and the number of oxygens, as in 18-crown-6. The lone pairs of the oxygens lining the inside of the ring coordinate to a cation, and because the outside is covered with ethylene groups, the complexes also dissolve readily in organic solvents. Compounds with fused benzene rings, such as dibenzo-18-crown-6, are also known.

A cation binds most strongly to the crown ether whose cavity matches its size. Typical cavity diameters are about 1.2–1.5 Å for 12-crown-4, about 1.7–2.2 Å for 15-crown-5 and about 2.6–3.2 Å for 18-crown-6, so 18-crown-6 fits K⁺, about 2.8 Å in diameter, well. The rings are flexible, however, and the strength of solvation also affects binding, so selectivity is not decided by size alone. With ions larger than the cavity, complexes in which two crown ether molecules sandwich the ion from above and below can also form.

Crown ethers take up the cations of salts and dissolve the salts in organic solvents in which they would not normally dissolve. Potassium permanganate, for example, dissolves in benzene in the presence of 18-crown-6 to give a purple solution. With the cation wrapped up, its association with the anion weakens, and since the anion is also poorly solvated, it behaves as a highly reactive "naked anion". Crown ethers are used in reactions that employ the fluoride ion of potassium fluoride as a nucleophile, and as phase-transfer catalysts.

faq.q: How do crown ethers differ from cryptands?
faq.a: A crown ether surrounds a cation with a flat single ring. A cryptand is cage-shaped, with two nitrogens joined by three chains, and wraps the cation in three dimensions, so it generally binds more strongly and selectively.

faq.q: How are crown ethers made?
faq.a: They are made by a Williamson-type ether synthesis in which an oligoethylene glycol and a compound with leaving groups at both ends are cyclized in the presence of a base. The template effect, in which the base's cation gathers the chain into a ring shape, raises the yield of cyclization.

faq.q: Are there precautions in handling them?
faq.a: Toxicity has been reported for some crown ethers, and they can be absorbed through the skin. Handle them with gloves and avoid inhaling them or getting them on the skin.

クリプタンド.desc: A cage-shaped ligand in which two nitrogens are joined by several polyether chains. It wraps a cation in three dimensions and binds it more strongly than a crown ether. The complex is called a cryptate.

シクロデキストリン.desc: An oligosaccharide of glucose units linked in a ring by α-1,4 bonds. Those with 6, 7 and 8 units are called α, β and γ, and they include organic molecules in their hydrophobic cavities.

自己組織化.desc: The spontaneous gathering of molecules or metal ions into a defined structure through reversible interactions. The system settles into the thermodynamically stable structure while correcting errors.

会合定数.desc: The equilibrium constant K = [HG]/([H][G]) for the association H + G ⇌ HG of a host H and a guest G. A measure of binding strength, related by ΔG° = −RT ln K.

about.p: When a host H and a guest G associate 1:1, as in H + G ⇌ HG, the equilibrium constant K = [HG]/([H][G]) is called the association constant (also the binding constant or stability constant); with concentrations in mol/L its unit is L/mol. Its reciprocal 1/K is the dissociation constant Kd, which has the dimension of concentration. The larger K, the stronger the binding; at 25℃ every 10-fold increase in K makes the standard Gibbs energy ΔG° = −RT ln K about 5.7 kJ/mol more negative. Values vary greatly with solvent, temperature and salt concentration.

Association constants are determined by titration, adding the guest in small portions to a solution of the host and following a physical quantity that changes on association. Changes in ¹H NMR chemical shifts, UV-Vis absorbance, fluorescence intensity and so on are fitted to an equation derived from the association equilibrium to determine K. Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) measures the heat released or absorbed with each addition and gives K and the enthalpy of association ΔH° simultaneously. For an accurate determination, a common guideline is to choose concentrations so that the bound fraction covers roughly the range 20–80%.

Before the analysis, the stoichiometry of the complex, whether 1:1, 1:2 or otherwise, needs to be checked. Job plots, which vary the mole fractions at constant total concentration, have long been used, but it has been pointed out that they readily give wrong conclusions when several complexes coexist. Today it is recommended to fit titration data with several models and judge by comparing the size and pattern of the residuals. Also, using an approximate equation that assumes a large excess of guest at concentrations where that condition does not hold gives large errors.

faq.q: When is the association constant used, and when the dissociation constant?
faq.a: They express the same equilibrium in opposite directions: Kd = 1/K. Supramolecular chemistry usually uses the association constant K (L/mol), and biochemistry and pharmaceutical science the dissociation constant Kd (mol/L); when the free guest concentration equals Kd, half of the host is bound.

faq.q: Why can't very large association constants be measured?
faq.a: When K is large, almost all the added guest binds, and the titration curve becomes like two straight lines that hardly depend on K. In that case the concentrations are lowered, or a displacement titration that competes with another, more strongly binding guest is used.

faq.q: Why does the association constant change with the solvent?
faq.a: On association, the host and guest each lose their interactions with the solvent. In strongly solvating solvents such as water or solvents that are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, association competes with solvation, so even the same pair can have association constants that differ by orders of magnitude.
